What portion of the estimates are we voting now ?
So much of the main estimates as we have passed upon in committee, and one-fifth of that portion of the estimates which have not been taken up.
Why is the need so urgent for passing these now ? We have only just reached the 1st of July, the financial year has only ended, and payments for the current year will not require to be made so early.

The invariable practice is, after resolutions have passed their various stages, to collect them in the first Supply Bill. We do not need the whole of them at once, I grant; if we had one-fifth of the whole it would be ample; but inasmuch as they have passed the committee, they are all included in the Bill. It is the usual course.

I regard the principle as an unsound one. The minister says we are adopting the usual course. It is a very unusual course. It is a very rare occurrence to pass a portion of the Supply Bill before the close of the session. I think I remember a few times when a small portion was voted, but it was only when the session was extended far beyond the usual length. You have practically the whole Supply Bill granted except a few items, so that at any time the government might avail themselves of the powers reserved to them without the permission of the House, and even though the opposition were not satisfied. It gives the control of the House into the hands of the government, I think improperly and unwisely for the safety of the country. I think we are establishing a very bad precedent.

I hope my hon.'friend will find, on examination, that we are not establishing any bad precedent ; and if it will make him any more bappy, I think I may go so far as to assure my hon. friend-though I would prefer that this came from the premier-that this House will not be dissolved before we proceed again in Committee of Supply. But as to the principle involved, it is not unusual to have a vote on account. It has been done time and again when the House has found itself in session after the 1st of July. If we had not passed any items in the estimates at all, we would have asked for one-fifth of everything; but it happens that a certain portion of the estimates had been dealt with, and they are included. Soon after the beginning of July, claims will come in, some of them very urgent, though not in every department; but it is convenient to take one-fifth of the whole rather than submit the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: estimates of the particular departments in which these urgent claims occur. Before this House will complete the Supply Bill, it will be necessary to pay certain claims. Take, for example, the Militia Department; there is urgent need for the payment of the militia now in camp. The course we are taking is with the single desire to meet the convenience of the public service, and there is no such danger as my hon. friend imagines.

If only one fifth were taken, it would not be so objectionable; but you have the whole of the supplies for public works, for railways and canals, for customs, and when this Bill goes through you will have practically the Supply Bill for the current year, though one of the main features of your policy, that with reference to the transcontinental railway scheme, is not yet before parliament. We are voting the supplies that will put us under the control of the government for the next year whether we will or not. Suppose we saw fit, after the government had submitted their policy to the House and the country, to refuse the Supply Bill. We could not help ourselves, because we have only held back a very small portion; and I regard it as an abandonment of the proper functions of the opposition to allow that to be done. I could understand the government requiring a small portion to keep the business of the country running; but I cannot understand why they should have practically' the whole of the supplies for the current year for public works, for railways, for canals, for militia, for customs, and other departments. After we have voted them, we are at the mercy of the government.

My hon. friend is wrong in assuming that we have taken so much of the estimates. As a matter of fact, a very large portion of the estimates have yet to be dealt with. We have not yet taken a penny of the estimates for railways, or for canals, or for the Interior Department, except for the past year.
We passed several items yesterday in connection with the Intercolonial Railway.

My hon. friend is mistaken. The Minister of Railways and Canals has not yet passed his estimates at all. These large spending departments have yet to bring the great bulk of their estimates before the House. The House will have ample opportunity of sitting in judgment on the expenditures of the government, and I have no doubt my hon. friend will avail himself of it.

speechtext: their duty. The fact that we have laid down a general provision does not warrant the inference that in all the subsequent sections we are dealing only with respect to railways that are to be constructed in the future. The language of the following clauses does not justify that interpretation. I must confess that I think my hon. friend 1 Mr. Cowan) is a little hypercritical about it. Let me deal with one or two suggestions he makes as to the phraseology cf the first section. The hon. gentleman would have us put in the word ' efficiently ' before the word ' drain.' They are bound to afford a sufficient outlet to carry off the water. I do not think you can add anything to make the meaning and intent any clearer.
You might drain off the water in a week, which is long enough to destroy a crop.

I do not think the outlet would be held to be sufficient if it would not carry off the water in a week. It should be sufficient to carry off the water in a reasonable time. The conditions might be so exceptional that no company could be supposed to anticipate such a demand on the outlet ; but if the outlet had been made sufficiently large to carry off the water under the ordinary conditions which prevail, without allowing the water to lie long enough to do any damage, it would be sufficient. My hon. friend must understand that these provisions are made with respect to conditions which exist not only in the county of Essex, but all over the country, wherever drainage is required. Where there is natural drainage going on when the railway is constructed, it is the business of the railway company to provide a sufficient outlet for that drainage. It is not necessary that they should make provision for artificial drainage, if there is not any or if the conditions are such as would not require it in other places, When we pass from the main clause of the section, we come to deal, not with the laying down of a general principle, but with the duties which attach to the railway company in the condition of things as they are to-day. These refer not simply to a railway which may be built after the passing of this Act, but to any railway wherever the trouble occurs and the remedy is being sought. But when we come to the next section, 195, we are drawing into the operations of this Act the provisions of the provincial law and applying them to the case that exists, so as to enable the landowner or the corporation that has drainage to proceed according to the practice laid down under that law and follow the remedy out to its conclusion. My hon. friend, I think, has indicated his satisfaction with that portion of the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not think we need have very much quarrel about section 194 ;

but section 195 is the important section, and if tbe bon. minister would change the word ' runs,' in the second line, so as to make it beyond all doubt apply to railways heretofore constructed as well as hereafter, I would have no fault to find with subsection 1 of that section.
Does my hon. friend say that these words, ' through which the railway runs,' would imply that the section had reference only to a railway to be run after the passage of this Act ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All I can say is the case I read the other day in volume 1 of the Ontario Reports of 1901, in which the Divisional Court of this province held that the words 1 is carried ' referred only to railroads constructed after the passing of the Act and not to railways constructed before; and when the hon. minister asks me if I think these words refer only to a railway to be constructed after the passing of this Act, I think it is a pretty close decision, stretching the words of the statute possibly further than the average legal mind would stretch them, but it has been done, and I think the words 'is carried' are just as strong as the words ' is run.'

I would not agree with my hon. friend in that. I think there is the clearest possible distinction between the case he refers to and the language of this clause. I am not going to venture to suggest that the decision is anything but right ; it is not necessary ; but if we were to make this section read ' is run,' then you would bring it within the judgment, at all events of that judge, and he would be bound, if he is to adhere to his original decision, to hold that the words had reference to a future act and not to conditions which exist to-day. But the distinction is very clear to my mind. All a judge has to ascertain and determine is : is there any railway running through that district to-day, at the moment when this remedy is applied ? When he finds that a railway is running, it is a matter of indifference to him when that railway was put through. I am quite sure that my hon. friend is wrong in that, and I think he will himself agree that there is no room for question when he thinks a little more about it. This clause is acceptable to my hon. friend with that one doubt in his mind. That being removed, the section, I take it, will meet with the approval of the committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would like to draw the minister's attention to this point. The clause provides that no drainage works shall be constructed until the character of such works, or the specification or plans thereof, shall have been first submitted to and approved by the board. Under section 16 of the Ditches and Watercourses Act of Ontario the engineer must make his report 194*
within thirty days, and he cannot make his award without the approval of the chief engineer of the railway commission ; or, if he does make the award, and approval is withheld by the commissioners, there is no machinery in the provincial legislation providing for the expense incurred, and the provincial statute will have to be amended to meet that case.

You will not have to amend any provincial Act. You will have to work out ] the matter in addition to what the provin-' cial Act requires. As respects Dominion railways, you cannot dig under them until the character of the work you have to perform has been approved by the board. There must be some superior tribunal to pass upon it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the hon. minister has made up his mind on that, so I accept that.
That does not require any amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Under the Ontario Act, if the engineer does not make his report within the thirty days the award is illegal. Furthermore, the moment the report of the engineer is adopted by the council, under our Drainage Act, he cannot change it, so that the Ontario statutes must be amended, which can be easily done.
I do not see any difficulty. When they have decided upon their scheme and have their plans, they need not wait until the work is under progress, but can send them into the board right at the start.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose the Railway Commission has approved plans submitted by the engineer, and which have been adopted by the council, the engineer cannot change his report or plan after their adoption. That has been definitely decided by the decisions of the courts.

Might I ask the hon. minister in what position would a municipality be which had made a drain that was afterwards crossed by a railway and which required to dredge out that drain ? Could the railway company be required to deepen that drain ?
That is probably the chief object for passing this clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It does not seem to me that it would apply to such a case. I know of instances where the railway companies refused to allow the municipalities to deepen the drain.

If the drainage originally provided is insufficient, this Bill enables an ap-

plication to be made to the Railway Commission, which would have the power to order the additional drainage. It would apply to every possible, conceivable condition and circumstance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have in my mind several cases of large drains which were constructed by the use of dredges and which must be kept In order and repaired by the same means. In many instances the railway companies have, since the construction of a drain, driven piles into them. If there be any such thing as right of way, the drains had that right in thq first instance. When the municipalitiles want toi repaifr those drains by dredges, they come up against the railway piles, and are prevented from doing so. What provision is there in the Bill to protect the rights of the municipalities ?
Application will have to be made to the Railway Commission, and that board will have jurisdiction to give an order compelling the railway companies to allow the drain to be repaired.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
At whose expense ?
The Minister of railways and
CANALS. That will be in the discretion of the board.
There ought to be some general principle laid down for the guidance of the board.

You have to leave these matters to the Railway Board, as we have hitherto left them to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, and I do not think that any fault has been found with the decisions of the Railway Committee. That committee has always found justification for making the railway company pay its proportion of the cost, if not the whole.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister know of any case in which the proportion can be fixed ?
We cannot arbitrarily fix a proportion. You have to leave the discretion somewhere, as you do in a court of equity. If you have not confidence in your tribunal, the whole system falls through.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not be reasonable to lay down some general rules or principle which would govern that tribunal ? Is it possible for the hon. gentleman to make such a provision that where the enlargement of the drain is made necessary by the railway company, the railway should bear the whole cost ? That is a fair proposition.
I know of one case where a railway company charged a dredging company, to take their dredge through
under the railway and bring it back, $1,500, which was almost as much as the drain cost. That is a couple of years ago.

If a farmer finds his land flooded, will he be able to start proceedings under this section to secure drainage ? If so, how will he do it ? What the farmers require is a simple method of draining their lands beneath the railways.

I do not know what the machinery is. All I can say is that lit is the same as that provided in the provincial Act. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Robinson) is better informed as to the Ontario law than I am.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You cannot get a drain through under that law.
I say that this section provides that the machinery shall be that provided by the provincial law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. minister did not understand me. I say that under the provincial law, you cannot get a drain across a railway, if the railway does not agree to your doing so.

The unfortunate part of my hon. friend's (Mr. Sproule's) condition is that, not having experience in law, he does not seem to know that with these companies you cannot now proceed under the provincial statute. But we provide here that the provincial law shall apply in these cases. What more can we do ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the provincial law is practically inoperative and of no value. If this law does not provide machinery for enforcing it, I do not see howl the farmers will be better off with respect to drainage than they are now.

As I understand it, this will make the Dominion railways subject to the control of the province as regards this matter. The Dominion railways in Ontario will be as much subject to the drainage laws of Ontario as a private owner would be with regard to his own lands.
Exactly.

Is the board of railway commissioners supposed to follow the law strictly, or have they discretionary power in that administration of it-that is, to make the law where there does not seem to be any special provision ? And would that be the case in such matters as that I referred to a moment ago ?

Many of the provisions of this law are imperative, while, in other things the form is permissive, and with respect to these the board has a good deal of discretion. It would be difficult to establish a good working system in every way. We

are attempting to provide a general administrative organization which shall have, from a railway point of view, control all over this country. One thing with another it is sought to enable the board to exercise its discretion with respect to the conditions which arise in different localities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But take such cases as I have spoken of where a large drain has been constructed before the advent of the railway, and the railway take possession of it. I think that case is sufficiently aggravated and of sufficient magnitude to be worthy of consideration by the hon. gentleman before coming to a final conclusion.

I have a good deal of difficulty in undertaking to give in words direction for guidance-not control-as to the different principles upon which the board is to act in these matters. If we attempted to provide for every case, I feel that we would be more likely to cause harm than to do good.
I am quite sure that if the board takes up a question of this kind, it will be far better able fo lay down principles for itself which will be equitable and just than we who have no knowledge of the circumstances and conditions. It does not follow that because this parliament establishes this board it loses legislative control. We shall be able to judge whether or not the machine lias been made fairly workable and where it has failed, if the difficulty is remediable, we can apply the remedy. While the perfect condition is the one to be desired, it is not to be looked for ; and, in seeking that perfection and trying to provide for every possible contingency, you would make stumbling blocks for your commission. That would be my fear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not know how it would be possible to frame any clause that would cover the hon. gentleman's case any better than this covers it:
The coat of the drainage or drainage work shall be in proportion to the benefit to he received by the company therefrom, unless the company shall have neglected to provide and maintain the necessary ditches and drains as in subsection 1 of the last preceding section is provided.
Now, it is a fair question as to whether that drainage which has been provided by the company is sufficient. The hon. gentleman is proposing to clear out the drain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am proposing to clear out a drain of which the company bore no share in constructing, and no claim is made upon them; and it would have to be admitted the railway company did not receive any benefit. It was a drain they took possession of, and they bore no part of the cost of its construction. Therefore, it does seem to me a piece of confiscation. You could not argue that they derived any benefit from it. Your whole case is that they prevented you from enjoying the benefits they had before the railway was constructed. So it does not come within the provisions of the section the hon. gentleman has read.

The hon. gentleman's provision is where drains cross the lands of a railway company. The case is simply reversed. In the one case the drain was constructed. There is no reason that you should make a distinction between a drain constructed as a watercourse and a natural watercourse. The hon. gentleman is placing a limit that should not exist. He knows that there are many drains that are not constructed through natural watercourses.

61S3
There is no drain in the county of Essex which has been constructed or repaired by a dredge, that is not a natural watercourse.
The hon. gentleman is speaking for his own county. I am speaking of things I am familiar with in other localities.
In the county of Essex all the drains are through natural watercourses where they cross the track.

There are drains in the county of Kent that are not natural watercourses at all, there are some even in the county of Essex. Take the lands where an embankment has been made in the county of Essex, through the plains where there were no watercourses in many cases.
Not under railways.

But I am showing that a railway might cross the drain. So it would be making an unfair limit to adopt the hon. gentleman's amendment and confine it to watercourses. If the hon. gentleman can get the Minister of Railways and Canals to accept his amendment, it ought to cover the case.

The question raised by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) has some similarity to a case in the county of Huntingdon. It is sometimes difficult to grasp these matters when we talk about them in the abstract; I want to put an actual case before the Minister of Railways and Canals, and to ask what should be done under the circumstances. We have in the county of Huntingdon what is called the Hall creek, which empties into the Chateauguay river, and runs altogether a distance of seven or eight miles. It crosses the New York Central Railw'ay, and where it crosses, the main branch was some nine feet wide. Last year we made a new procSs-verbal, as we call it, to drain that land. Some of the land had been cleared up, and we found we had to change the main channel of the creek. We removed it west a mile or a mile and a half. There had been a branch of the creek across the railway at that particular place, which was only four feet wide, and we made it nine feet wide and made it a main discharge, making it the same width as the original discharge, nine feet, and making at what was the original discharge a branch four feet wide. The New York Central had a wooden culvert four feet wide, and we required a culvert nine feet wide. That culvert has not yet been built and we want them to build it. They intend to put in a concrete culvert nine feet wide, and I understand that under one of the sections of the hon. gentleman's Bill the cost of these culverts should be borne in proportion to the benefits received by the various properties drained and the railway. Under these circumstances what proportion does the min-

ister think should be borne by the railway, and what proportion by the farmers ? This is a concrete case, and I would like to know how we stand. I may say our contention is that the railway should put in that new culvert, and they intended to do it as the law stands now. But if this new Act is passed, I am afraid the New York Central will come to the municipality of which I am secretary-treasurer, and want us to pay part of the price of that new culvert, which I do not think we have any right to pay for. There is were we stand, and 1 want the minister to answer my question.
My mind is not working actively on abstract questions of damages.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is not a question of damages.
I would not like to answer the hon. gentleman's question off-hand. I think if I did he would not think very much of the opinion I gave. The facts would have to be inquired into.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If I understand the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals he is bringing in a railway Bill and he is undertaking to frame a particular section to deal with these matters. ' I say it is a concrete question, not an abstract question. I would like to know what the hon. minister had in his mind when he framed the section and how he would apply it to this case. My contention is that when a railway runs through a country and builds up a bank which interferes with the drainage it is bound to give openings through or under that railway which would give the farmers as good drainage as they would have had if the railway had not been built. That particular railway of which I spoke crossed a man's farm. This man had a farm which was forty rods wide. The right of way cost the company at the rate of $75 an* acre, or about $50 for crossing the farm. Does anybody mean to tell me that that is any compensation to this farmer for the damage that has been done to him by the building of that railway ? My contention is that if a railway company obstruct the drainage of the country and if culverts and openings are required for the farmers such drainage should be at the expense of the railway company and the farmers should not be required to pay any proportion of it. That is the ground I take, because, if you say, as in the section, that the railway company has to pay proportionate to the benefit received, what benefit does the railway receive by having a culvert pass under it ? The difficulty we have in getting drainage is that the railway companies say that it is injurious, that they do not consider it any benefit, but that they consider it a nuisance and they fight us in every way possible to prevent us getting drainage

across their lands to the natural outlets which would have been clear of any obstacle had the railway not been constructed.

The railway companies contend that they receive no benefit from drainage and that it will be a damage to them instead of a benefit. I know of a place where a man carried his drains down through another farm to get to the outlet. He had to build the drain for a third of a mile to get to the outlet, where 150 feet would have taken him to the outlet if the railway had not been there. He had to go to this extra expense on account of the railway. He could have put the tile under the railway and the water would have run through that without any great expense if the railway had thought fit to consent to allow him to do so.

I have not been able to see the proposed amendments until just now and I find by looking at these amendments that they do not meet the difficulties at all, at least, some of the difficulties that were presented the other day. The Ontario Ditches and Watercourses Act as applied to railways, provides that all the cost of putting necessary drainage under railway lands shall be borne by the parties making the application and nothing paid by the company. That is expressly provided in the Railway Ditches and Watercourses Act of Ontario. It was pointed out very forcibly by the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment the other day and others who followed him that it was only fair that the landowner should be put in the position that lie would have been in if the railway had not been carried across his lands. I find that in subsection 2 of section 195, as it is now proposed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, the following words :
The proportion of the cost to be borne by the company of the construction or reconstruction or maintenance of any such drainage or drainage works, so required to be constructed, reconstructed or maintained upon, along, under or across the railway or lands of the company shall be in proportion to the benefit to be received by the company therefrom unless the company shall have neglected to provide and maintain the necessary ditches and drains, as in subsection one of the last preceding section provided.
As T understand that section it amounts to this, that we are proceeding upon the basis that each party lias only to pay in proportion to the benefit that will be derived. That is the principle that is laid down for the guidance of the board and that is tlie rule that is to be adopted. We are not dealing with a case of where two parties are seeking to have an apportionment of benefit decided between them. We are dealing with a case where the landowner is suffering under the grievance created solely by the railway company. The railway company want to do nothing whatever. They want to stand as they are. The landowner is endeavouring to get rid of this grievance. It will be a benefit to him to get rid of this grievance, but it will only be a benefit which will in the end restore him to the condition in which he would have been if there had been no railway built at all. When you speak of the benefit he would derive it is merely that his rights are being restored to him under the Act for this he should not have to pay. He should have his rights restored under this Act without condition and without expense and until that is done justice is not done to the landowner. The true principle was enunciated (he other day by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) and I wonder he is not ready to maintain it today, or has not been so far, that we should replace the landowner in as good a position as he was in before the railway was constructed. That is all we are asking, but if you are to measure it by the benefit derived, as I ventured to point out the other day, the logical answer of the railway company is : We are not getting any benefit, we are in a better position if no drainage is carried underneath our railway, every cutting under the railway weakens the roadbed. Even if it can be done for nothing, we are rather injured than benefited. But, the answer of the farmer is : I want to get my lands restored to the condition of usefulness they were in before. If you provide in the section that it will be in proportion to the benefit derived, then no court having regard to the ordinary meaning of language can do anything else than exonerate the railway completely from payment, because the wording is ' in proportion to the benefit ' and the railway company can certainly say that they are deriving no benefit from the work. Let me direct the hon. minister's attention to the position of the matter. By the wording of this section a sufficient remedy is not provided. Means are probably provided for getting drainage under the railway lands, but certainly at the expense of the person -who makes the application because not one dollar of it will be paid by the railway company. When you invoke the provincial Act in the province of Ontario, and I think the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) explained the other day that the law is similar in the province of Quebec, all the expenses are paid by the municipalities to the railway company. The minister has evidently taken a considerable amount of pains in recasting this legislation, and while I call attention to this point I want to say that in the main I believe the provisions are satisfactory. But in this particular I submit with due respect that they do not improve the conditions as they existed before.

I am prepared to say that a railway company could get no benefit, but if they got any benefit that benefit should be 1 deducted from any sum which they would

be required to pay, or rather, they would have to make allowance for that benefit when the question of ccsts came to be fixed. You must start out with the fact that the duty of the railway company is at the time it constructs its line to have provided all proper drainage. Having done that, and if ditches are required to be enlarged by reason of changed conditions since the railway was constructed, I do net think they should be asked to assume all the expense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why not?
Why should not those interested in the drainage bear their share of the burdens which are imposed by the altered conditions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There would be no increased cost if the railway was not there.
You would have to enlarge your ditches:
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The enlarging of the ditches would cost $1 or ?f>. What I refer to is a culvert which would cost $500 and which would not be necessary if the railway was not there.

In the original Bill introduced by me it was provided that the proportion of the cost of the drain crossing a railway, to be borne by the railway company, should be based upon the increased cost of such work caused by the construction and operation of that railway. The reason why the railway company should bear that proportion is, that when the railway company went through these lands they knew that in order that these lands might be properly tilled they must be properly drained. They also knew that the fall of the land lay across their right of way, and in order to properly till and drain the land there must be openings under the railway sufficient to carry oft' the water. Therefore, in the construction of the road-bed, if they failed to leave these culverts or openings they should pay the increased cost by reason of their failure to do so. When a railway goes through an absolutely new section of the country there are no farm crossings required, but still the law provides that the railway company must give them farm crossings, because when they clear the land it will be necessary for the farmer to pass from one side to the other. The Act says that these farm crossings shall be made at the expense of the railway company. If it is necessary in the case of farm crossings, much more so is it necessary where it is absolutely impossible to till the land. Unless openings or culverts pass under the railway as the natural lay of the land requires for the necessary drainage thereof, as in the state of Illinois, pro-
vision should be made by the railway ct m-pany. ' Sufficient for the necessary drainage thereof.'

When lands are being expropriated for a railway company it is necessary to file plans and profiles of the track showing the embankments across the line and so on. Then the appraisers go upon tlie land and they estimate the value of that land and also the damage occasioned to the owner by severance, and in estimating that they say that the adjoining land is uncultivated, but if at any future time it may be cultivated then the railway company must give farm crossings. But a different principle prevails with regard to this drainage. The appraisers say that so far as the drainage is concerned there is no further burden laid upon the railway in that regard. Therefore the two eases are not parallel. In one case they have it distinctly before them that the railway company can be compelled to construct crossings, but they cannot be compelled in some cases to construct an opening across the track for drainage. Suppose the railway company has constructed a railway and has put in drains sufficient for carrying out the natural flow of the water if a system of drainage is afterwards constructed by the farmers in the locality which increases the flow of water at a certain point, that is done to enhance the value of their property and it seems to me that should be taken into consideration.
Does it not enhance the value of the property of the railway Company by giving it increased freight ?
That is a very pertinent remark, and if by reason of that work the company obtains more revenue, then that should be taken into consideration also.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister to this section. The persons claiming drainage would be infinitely better without that provision, because unless they are prepared to show that the railway company benefits from the drainage works, it would not be required to bear any share of the cost. I would ask the hon. gentleman, if he were sitting as a judge, and a case came before him under this section, and the landowners could not show that the railway company derived a benefit from the maintenance of a drain already constructed before they took possession of it, would he not decide that the landowners would have to pay the whole cost of cutting through the railway, and the railway company none ?
That would depend on whether or not they had constructed a sufficient drain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Suppose the railway company had no mandate to construct drains

at all, but the railway crossed a large drain. It would be simply impossible to show that the railway company derived any benefit from it or was the least concerned In it, beyond having prevented the landowner getting through. According to the provisions of this section, before the railway company are called upon to bear any share of the cost, it must be shown that they have derived some benefit from the work. The landowners would be infinitely better without such a provision, leaving the matter an open question. I do not know any more serious* phase of the bon. gentleman's legislation than this. 1 am sure that every lawyer will see that it is a most dangerous thing. It puts us out of court entirely.

When the railway company permits a drain to cross the railway, the municipality or the landowner lias to pay the cost, and this includes the cost of engineers and other expenses, which are sometimes more than the cost of the culvert itself. I know of one culvert in the hon. gentleman's own riding (Botliwell) which cost the township of Chatham $5,000 under the management of the railway company, whereas if the municipality had put it in, I do not think it would have cost more than $1,000 ; so that the railway company injured the municipality to the extent of $4,000, and kept the water back and drowned out the crops for a number of years besides.
Will the minister kindly tell us just what portion of the cost he proposes that the railway company shall bear, under subsection 2 of section 195 ?
I propose that if they are not in default they shall pay no portion unless they get the benefit.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The clause goes further than that. It refers to railways already constructed.

No, to all railways. Many of us are disposed to think that we can fall back on the railway companies with perfect reason and propriety to bear the cost ; but I think it is at least reasonable that we should consider that all railways are not a source of injury and destruction to the countries through which they pass.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The bon. gentleman surely will not make an argument of that kind. No one has said so.	-

I think some little recognition should be given to the fact that railways are very necessary and useful institutions, and in a great majority of cases very much enhance the value of the property though which they pass, often making valuable land
which before was nothing but a wilderness. We have heard a gcod deal about the superiority of the Ontario law, and my bon. friend has availed himself of the provisions of that law. If I understand the provisions of the Ontario Act as they relate to ordinary landowners, and their rights in regard to draining, this principle obtains, that where the drain benefits the land, the landowner must pay in proportion to the benefit he derives towards the cost. of the construction of the drain. I believe the railway companies pay nothing ; they are not asked to make any contribution at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can tell the hon. gentleman that in certain localities they do not pay a farthing.

That is what I am stating. Under the Ontario law, when drains are put through under these drainage commissions, the railway company makes no contribution whatever. We are rather improving upon the Ontario legislation, which is recognized by our hon. friends opposite as being very superior and worthy of being followed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I want to say that it is enough to exhaust the patience of this committee to listen to the reasons which the hon. gentleman has given. If the hon. gentleman were the advocate of the railways of thiis country, he could not take a different position from what he has taken just now. It is the most extraordinary thing you could expect from a minister of the Crown and a gentleman of his large experience as a parliamentarian and a lawyer, to say that a man through whose land the railway runs should suffer all .these penalties by reason of that fact. No one has contended in this committee that railway companies should not have the right to expropriate, and the hon. gentleman must be driven to the last ditch when he makes such a plea in favour of this legislation. I tell the hon. gentleman that with his eyes open he is introducing a manifest injustice into our railway legislation by the clause he asks us to pass. He is taking even from the board of commissioners the right to do justice to the farmers. He affects to believe that the railway companies contribute to the drains, but he must know that they do not contribute a farthing. The only drains, for the construction of which they have paid, are those which cross their own lands or which are made in order to provide outlets for drains upon their own lands. But in cases where drains have been built by municipalities or private landowners and are obstructed by railway companies, the hon. gentleman says that unless you can show that the particular railway company interested is benefited, the farmers must pay the -whole cost of repairing such drains. I know of no more deliberate piece of robbery than is involved in the section the hon. gentleman has in his Bill.

I must admit that when the amendments were read this afternoon, I dad not follow them very closely, because I knew that the hou. member for Essex was giving special attention to the matter, but I am perfectly amazed, when I come to read those amendments, which, by the way, it was understood we were to have had copies of in advance. I am astonished that the hon. minister could so far overlook the relative rights of the parties as to have submitted the proposition which we find in the concluding words of section 395, subsection 2. Instead of giving us some measure of relief, he is putting the farmers and the landowners adjoining railways in an infinitely worse position than if he had done nothing. The other day I endeavoured to have these matters settled by the local tribunals, and in that view I ventured to point out that it would be well to invoke provincial legislation. But I also pointed out that so far as the province of Ontario was concerned, the legislation of that province would lead to this result, that the railways probably would escape all liability.

The hon. gentleman seems to think that this subsection makes their position a great deal worse than before. Let me say that if the hon. member for Essex is willing to have subsection 2 struck out from section 195, I am willing to drop it altogether.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Some hon. gentlemen on the other side, notably the hon. member for Simcoe, have seen fit to refer to me once or twice as sitting silent while some iniquitous legislation was being passed, and have suggested that I was not pursuing the course to-day that I did on a former occasion. Let me say to the hon. member for Simcoe that I was discussing clause 195.

I rise to a point of order.
I merely resumed my seat in order to allow the hon. Minister of Railways to interrupt me by some remarks which he desired to make, and I do not propose to give up my place to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan). I should be very glad to accept any suggestion that will facilitate the progress of this business, and I hope that the hon. member for Essex does not consider that it is from any desire to be lacking in courtesy that I wish to proceed with my observations.

If the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) will permit me-I am sure of that in his case. But I wish to explain that I was discussing section 195. I have an amendment to propose in substitution of that subsection 2, for that subsection does not suit me.

Under these circumstances I think the proper course for me will be to curtail my remarks, for I may entirely agree with the amendment to be proposed. I am not opposing this nor are any Mr. CLANCY.
of us opposing it, with a view to political effect. We are all on the same line, though we may not view it in the same way. We want to secure fair play for the railway companies, but we want also fair play for the people. I represent a rural constituency, and my sympathies are naturally with the people in rural localities. But I have a special reason for the position I take. The first railway line projected in Canada, barring a short line in Quebec, runs through my riding. It was built in 1851, and the ponds caused by the embankments of that railway are there undrained to this day. So, I have reason to know the sentiment of the people on this question. If we adopt the local law of Ontario without any qualification, we get into this condition. We have the Ordinary Ditches and Watercourses Act, and we have also the Railway Ditches and Watercourses Act, which is to be x-ead as part of the other. Now, after provisions for the meeting of the engineers, the estimate of the cost and everything in connection with putting a drain under the railway, the law reads :
But the railway company shall not be liable for the cost of any work performed upon lands or under the road-bed of any railway under the provisions of this Act.
It is said by the hon. minister that we from Ontario were proud of our legislation, and boast of it. So we are in some respects. But, if the hon. minister reads the discussion of this point in this House, he will see that I, at all events, contended that we must be careful as regards this provision, as, otherwise, the railway company would escape liability, whereas the very principle enunciated by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) was that all the additional cost occasioned by the presence of the railway should be borne by the railway company, so that the parties might be restored to their original positions. I reserve any further remarks until I have heard the amendment of the hon. member for South Essex.

Subsection 2, of section 195, as it is now proposed, means, if I read it con'ectly, that if a railway, at the time of its construction, neglected to leave the proper openings for culverts to drain the land as it was then, the increased cost of drainage occasioned by its construction over and above what it would have been if it had made these openings, is to be borne by tlie farmers. I shall not extend my re-mai'ks to show again why the railway company ought.to bear the inci'eased cost occasioned by the construction of its roads, but shall simply submit the amendment I have prepared. I propose that the following be substituted for subsection 2, of section 195 :
The proportion of the cost of the drain or drainage works across or upon the railway to be borne by the railway company shall in all cases be based upon the increase of cost of

such works caused by the construction and operation of the railway.
That puts the matter as clearly, I think, as the English language can put it, and it is briefly this that whatever it would cost to take that ditch across the land occupied by the line of the railway, if there were no railway works there, shall be borne by the farmer. For example, if it would cost $5 to take the drain across the land in the absence of any railway works, that $5 shall be paid by the farmer. But if the construction of the road-bed causes the work of crossing the land occupied by that roadbed to be $50, the railway shall bear the $45 and the farmer the $5. That is, the increased cost which the construction of the railway has occasioned in the making of the drain shall be borne by the railway. That is as clear as I can put it, and I hope the House will understand it.

I asked the Minister of Railways a question, and he did not answer to my satisfaction. I desire to propose an amendment in the following language :
That wherever it is found that farm lands are injured by the overflow of water caused by the construction of a railway, the railway commissioners shall have power and shall provide and compel said railway companies to construct drains sufficient to carry off all waters, natural and artificial, at the expense of the railway companies.

Referring to the amendment of the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan), I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to one point. Suppose that a railway is constructed through a certain section of the country. The openings allowed for the passage of water are quite sufficient, for all the purposes of the railway at the time of construction. But, five or six years after this the municipal council decides to drain the whole municipal area. It constructs a drain-in some counties these drains are more like canals, being eight or ten miles long-and brings it down to the railway and wants to cross the railway, On what principle of justice should the railway company be called upon to pay the extra cost that is necessary to take that drain across the railway ? I cannot understand that. The work may be a useful and necessary one for the community, but I cannot understand why the railway should be compelled to bear this extra cost. As long as means are provided and instructions given to the Railway Commission that upon any reasonable grounds the drain shall have the right of passage, I think that is sufficient. They should not be compelled by statutory enactment to pay for the increased cost qf the construction of that work.

I wish to point out to my hon. friend from Essex that he has not well considered his amendment, for he does not even make provision for the case where a railway company has taken land in the first instance, and has fully settled for it and made compensation. My hon. friend' would make the railway pay irrespective of whether they had made compensation or not.
Amendment (Mr. Cowan) agreed to.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext: On the order for resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Campbell, that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 147) to incorporate the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Company.

Mr. Speaker. The attention of the government has been called to the fact that very strong objections are entertained to further proceeding with this Bill on the ground that the Bill assumes to take legislative control in respect to a local measure out of the hands of the provincial legislature of Ontario. It is maintained that it is open to objection on various grounds, not simply because it is a usurpation by this parliament of a subject that properly belongs to the provincial legislature, but, because the exercise of authority by this parliament over the Bill would be to withdraw an undertaking of this character from the supervision, regulation and control of the province. The government is desirous that the measure should not be proceeded with to-night and I would ask that it stand with the view of hearing from those gentlemen who are here now and who wish to present their objections to the Bill. I think I may say with authority that if it appears from what may be stated to us by these gentlemen that this is not properly a subject for us to legislate upon and that we are in fact withdrawing from the provincial legislature control over a railway which ought to be permitted to remain within the provincial control, the government will not sanction or permit the Bill to pass. We ask now that it may stand for the purpose which I have mentioned. I beg to move that the debate be now adjourned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister who has just spoken (Hon. Mr. Blair) if the Bill is to be proceeded with that we will get notice in time to give notice of certain amendments that we desire to make.
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 175) respecting the Century Life Insurance Company-Mr. Morrison.

That Bill No. 175 be amended by adding the following -section at the end of the printed Bill * Clause 3, paragraph 4, chapter 93, 1 Ed. VII, is hereby amended by substituting in the secoud line the word ' ten ' instead of the word 'twenty-five.'

Mr. Chairman, I do not understand that chapter 93, I Edward VII, is before this committee at all. I fail to see how we are going to amend a Bill that has never come before us. Had the amendment been to change or add to Bill 175 I could see the force of it, but I fail to see why or how we can amend a Bill that was passed last session without any notice whatever being given other than that which appears in the Votes and Proceedings. The Bill of last year is not before us and is therefore not open to amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member's point is not well taken. I think we are doing something similar to this almost every day, amending Acts of parliament that are not before us. This is simply proposing to amend an Act of parliament to which the hon. gentleman refers by making a change of these words of ' ten ' for 'twenty five.' Therefore, the Act which is now before us will be amended by the passage of this clause.
Every Act is before us.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Act is in a sense before us to-night.

While I do not wish to press unduly the objection it seems to me that this is a most irregular proceeding. I might as well give notice that when Bill 175 is taken up I will move an amendment to some Bill that was passed ten years ago and that has no relevancy whatever to the matter before the committee. No notice of it came before the Committee on Standing Orders. They knew nothing about it, and I would like to know from a member of the government whether he thinks this is a regular proceeding.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson), in his illustration, is hardly fair in saying that we might as well undertake to amend a Bill passed ten years ago having no relevancy whatever to the Bill before the House. This Bill has relevancy inasmuch as the Act which it is proposed to amend is an Act relating to the same company. Therefore, there is nothing irrelevant in it.

speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
I would agree with the Minister of Finance if we had a Bill
before us to amend the Bill referred to in the notice of motion, but I fail to see anything in the nature of an amendment.

The whole Act is one respecting the Century Insurance Company and one section of that Act is referred to in this Bill as being amended. Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) can see the difference between that, and the reference to an Act that had no relevancy to the one in question. The object of the amendment is to reduce the amount that is to be paid upon organization.

We have here a Bill which originally consisted of one section, but now it has grown into a Bill of a great many sections. It appears to me that under the circumstances this Bill should be reprinted and redistributed, or else, liow are the members of this House to know what it is about and to vote intelligently on it. In the case of these Bills which are considerably altered they should be reprinted. I would like to have the opinion of one of the ministers as to that.
This Bill was fully considered in committee and the amendment was not opposed. If there is to be any very strong objection to it, it would be better to refer the Bill back to committee.
I did not so much need the opinion of a prospective minister as an actual minister of the Crown at the present time.

Hear, hear.
ilr. LENNOX. The majority of the members of this House have not the honour to belong to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and so it is impossible for us to know what changes have been made in the Bill.

1 am quite satisfied that the Bill in its present shape is innocent, but if any hon. gentleman desires to have it reprinted I have no objection. The company came before us with a single clause proposing to extend their time for organization for one year. When the Bill was passing through the committee on Banking and Commerce it was deemed well to introduce clauses which have been introduced into the legislation of other companies since this charter was obtained, so that we might put them on even terms with other companies chartered last session and this session. My hon. friend (Mr. Morrison) comes in now with a further suggestion which has not been before the committee, but which is in crnformity with what has been done in other charters, and I do not suppose there would be any harm in permitting the company to do the same thing as others. In the charters of one or two other companies permission has been given for them to

change their name under certain circumstances, and it is proposed that the same power shall be given to this comrany. There is nothing in this Bill as it now stands thaf is not to be found in the legislation granted to other companies.

I may say that these clauses were inserted in the committee at the instance of the Minister of Finance who proposes to insert similar clauses in all charters of this kind, and so far as the company is concerned that was done against their assent. Clause 4 simply gives the company the right to change its name with the approval of the Governor in Council, a provision which is to be found in the charters of other life Insurance companies, and the next clause simply safeguards the public so that the change of name shall not affect the obligations of the company. I cannot see that there can be any objection to that.

I am perfectly willing to take the explanation of the Minister of Finance, made much stronger and better of course by the explanation of the leader of the opposition, but I take the general objection that when a Bill of this kind is brought before us it should be printed so that we may know what its provisions are and not be' obliged to vote for it in the dark. I call the attention of the government to the matter in order, that they should take steps to prevent such a thing occurring in the future.

I entirely concur in the suggestion of the hon. member for West York that this Bill be referred back to the Banking and Commerce Committee for further consideration. The original Bill merely provided a year's extension for the company to procure its license. That was all that was considered by the committee. Now we have another and even more important amendment proposed, not to the Bill, but to the original charter of the company,-a change which has not been considered by the Banking and Commerce Committee. If there was any useful purpose served by sending the Bill in the first instance to the Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce, why is it not just as advisable and necessary to send this new and important proposed provision of the Bill to be considered by the committee ? At the same time, if the Bill is sent back to the committee, I think it would be well to make some inquiry into the history of the company. I am informed that there were serious complaints made against the passage of the original Bill granting the extension of time, by the people who may be termed stockholders of the company, and I think these complaints merit a little more consideration than they have received. I move that this Bill be referred back to the Committee on Banking ahd Commerce.

speechtext: 1 must inform the hon. gentleman that the motion is not in order, as it has not been made in the proper place. That motion should have been made when the order was read by the clerk at the Table before we went into committee. My hon. friend who has just spoken has on a previous occasion made the reference that he has made at the present time, and the sense of the committee was adverse *to the suggestion he made on that occasion. My hon. friend also had the opportunity before the committee to lodge any complaints which he might have had in regard to the details of the measure. The committee considered the Bill fully, the House considered it and passed upon it, and now my hon. friend comes a second time without any new argument and asks that the time of the committee and of this House be taken up in considering a matter which has already been fully gone into by the Minister of Finance and by the officers connected with the Banking and Commerce Committee. I cannot see that there is any force in such a request, and I would strongly urge that no more time be taken up in a matter which after all has not been shown to be of' any consequence, and that this Bill be allowed to pass. I must confess, as the hon. Minister of Finance has said, that there has been considerable patchwork about the Bill, but that is the fault of the solicitors who have charge of it. I think there has been nothing done but what should have been done by the officers of the committee in seeing that the interests of the public were safeguarded. The government have seen tit to add two clauses, and then it was discovered by those in charge of the Bill that these two omissions had been made, and these two paragraphs are added. They do not affect the subsl^nce of the Bill, and I would strongly urge that it be allowed to pass as amended.
