House in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.
On section 196-farm crossings.

I move that the following words be added :
And whenever the embankment and road-bed of the railway is high enough to permit of its being done, the railway company shall make

undercrossings, passing beneath the track, built up of stone or other material, for the convenience of persons across whose land the railway is carried, in order to permit the passage of live stock back and forth, such under-crossings to be maintained and kept in repair by the railway company.
My object is to anticipate what may be a serious grievance in the future, just as we have been anticipating serious grievances with regard to drainage. Let me cite to the committee a circumstance which will show the necessity for this amendment. On the line of the London, Huron & Bruce Railway, which happens to be a branch of the Grand Trunk Railway, a number of farmers enjoyed for a considerable length of time under crossings. They enjoyed them as a right from the railway company in harmony with an agreement made by that company with tlie individuals. The agreement was made some twenty-live years ago and was drawn up by an hon. member of this House, who is consequently familiar with the circumstances. The railway company lived up to that agreement for twenty-five years, but during the past year, for some reason or other, it has filled up those under crossings, very much to the detriment of the farmers over whose laud the railway passes. In the future construction of railways, a precaution of that kind ought to be provided, because it is a very serious matter to a farmer to have to drive his cattle across a railway instead of under it. Where a farm is crossed by a railway with a number of level crossings, that involves serious risk to him in driving his cattle back and forth. I brought this case particularly to the attention of the hon. minister, who promised to consider it; and it seems to me that in anticipation of difficulties of that kind in the future, some provision should be made for the placing of .under crossings in the formation of the roadbed. I do not wish to convey the idea that all the under crossings on the line of the London, Huron & Bruce have been filled in, but certainly some have, very much to the injury of the farmers. The excuse given by the company for violating its agreement is that this agreement,was not embodied m the deed of transfer of the property from the farmers to the company and not registered, and therefore they claim that they are under no obligation to maintain these under crossings, although they admitted their own liability by keeping them in a state of repair for twenty-five years. It seems to me that a provision of this kind would contribute also to the safety of the travelling public by providing against cattle being struck by passing trains and thereby endangering the safety of the passengers.
I understood that the hon. minister had an amendment to propose to tins clause, which would give the right ''l farmers to have crossings over portions ot their land, in cases where a part had been

disposed of and a part retained. A man, for instance, who has one hundred acres, might sell fifty acres. It might happen that the crossing was on the part sold, and because thei law only obliges railway companies to give one crossing over a lot, they could refuse to furnish another crossing or to allow another to be built on that portion of the lot remaining unsold. I understood that the hon. minister intended proposing an amendment to meet such a case, and it would be more proper to deal with that now before considering the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes).

I have prepared an amendment with regard to level crossings, which perhaps the hon. member for West Huron would accept as being more practical than his own. It would impose a heavy burden on the railway company to compel them to tunnel under their roads every quarter of a1 mile or so. It would almost amount to reconstructing the whole roadbed, and although that might be in the interest of the farmers, it might; also be unreasonable. What I was going to propose was the following amendment :
That section 196 be amended by adding after the word ' accidents ' in the last line of such section the words ' and the company shall erect and maintain fences of the minimum height of four feet six inches on each side of the crossing from the company's boundary fences to points as near to each side of the rails as to admit of the safe passage of trains.
That perhaps would meet with the approval of the hon. minister. Even if the railways do not agree to it, it is an obligation which we have the right to impose on them. The remedy proposed by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) is to compel the railways to provide passage for the animals underneath, but we ought not to impose burdens on railways which are not absolutely necessary, and the plan I suggest would be cheaper and accomplish the same result. It may be known to some lion, members that during tlie recess, I was attending many meetings of the cattle-guard commission, and it is but right that I should tell the House that although the farmers were very anxious to get that law amended, they also were urging upon me to get the farm crossings protected in some such way as I am providing. I would point out also that the hon. minister, in drawing up this measure, has imposed a burden upon the farmers with regard to farm crossings which does not exist to-day.
The law which is now in force, and which will be in force until this parliament prorogues, simply provides that ' every company shall make the crossings for persons across whose lands the railway is carried, convenient and proper for the crossing of the railway by farmers' implements, carts and other vehicles.' Under the law as the I lion, minister proposes to amend it, pro-

vision is made that ' every company shall make crossings for persons across whose lands the railway is carried, convenient and proper for the crossings of the railway for farm purposes.' The word ' vehicles ' is not used. And this provision is added :	' In
crossing with live stock, the same shall be in charge of some competent person, who shall use all reasonable care and precaution to avoid accidents.' Of course, we presume that every person will use care and precaution, but here is a distinct addition to the law, laying it down as an emphatic command to the farmer that care and precaution shall be used. But while we impose it upon the farmer that he shall use proper precautions with regard to live stock, we ought to compel the railway to use proper precautions also. Both parties ought to be compelled, or induced, so far as we can control them, to do everything reasonably possible to prevent the impact between animals and the trains. But it is not only at farm crossings that cattle and the trains come in contact. As the law stands, it is not necessary for the railway company to do anything but to have its line fenced between its right of way and the adjoining farm property. While the gate of the farm *crossing is open for animals to pass, they have access to the whole width of the right of way. There is no immediate danger except at that point. But the animals are apt to turn to the right or left as soon as they get through the gate, and they have the lands of the railway between the fence and the track to run upon. They have to be headed off and driven back. But they may meet a train at any moment. If there were fences set at right angles to the boundary fence and carried down as far as would be consistent with the safe passage of trains, the danger from these cattle getting upon the railway right of way would be reduced to a minimum, because they could only escape where the rails are. In the case of highway crossings, there will be cattle-guards. I am not suggesting that there should be cattle-guards at the farm crossings, but I am only saying that we should reduce the chances of danger as far as we can. While we impose this additional clause upon th,e farmer, bringing it in this year for the first title, providing that the farmer is to have his animals under the care of a competent person who shall take all reasonable care and precaution to avoid accidents, we ought to impose upon the railways the duty of doing all that is reasonably possible to assist the farmer in preventing accidents. It would be a matter of small expense to carry the fences out at right angles to as near the rails as would be consistent with the safe passage of trains. That is why I propose this amendment. It is not an undue or unreasonable imposition upon the railway. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) is designed to accomplish the same
end and remedy the same grievance. PerI haps the hon. gentleman will come to the conclusion that my amendment will accomplish what we both want, and it lias the additional advantage, as I regard it, that the expense will be merely trifling as compared with his proposal of tunnelling under the railways at each farm crossing, which might be every eighth cr quarter of a mile.

Three or four subsections have been dealt with by hon. members ; I shall try to deal with them in the order in which they have been brought up. The hon. member for Easit Grey (Mr. Sproule) called attention to the case of farms being split up and portions sold, and suggested the making of additional farm crossings. I think the hon. member must have misunderstood me if he thought that I had engaged to prepare an amendment on the subsection. 1 did engage to turn the matter over in my mind to see whether the proposition that the hon. gentleman made could be accepted. I have considered the matter, but have not been able to see that it would be reasonable or fair to multiply these farm crossings to the extent that would be necessary if the suggestion were given effect to. It is possible that a farm might be cut up into half a dozen parts and distributed among as many diherent owners. We know that that is very much the practice in the province of Quebec, where the farms are very narrow. A railway might pass eight or ten times as many crossings as were originally provided for, by reason of the property being divided and passing into different hands. That, I think, would be an exceedingly onerous obligation to impose upon the railway. I think that it would also multiply the danger involved in operating the railway. On consideration, it does not strike me that we ought to require this of the company. It is always possible for the owner of a farm, if he decides to sell, to afford opportunity to the person to whom he sells to use his crossing. I think it would be better to require that that should be done rather than to multiply farm crossings and increase the hazzards involved.
Now we come to the further vexed question, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). I think that is a very serious proposition. 1 must confess that it does not commend itself to my mind. I think we are carrying this sort of legislation pretty far and are imposing very heavy and expensive obligations upon the railway companies which they have not hitherto been called upon to bear.
I am not saying that we have already gone too far, but I am saying that we had better proceed a little more deliberately. We had better see how what we have already effected works, and, perhaps, later, this or a cognate proposition might be considered by parliament. But at this stage, not hav-

mg been able to give to the subject proper consideration, not having heard what may be alleged on the other side, I think I would not be justified in acceding to the hon. gentleman's request or asking the committee to entertain it.
My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has a suggestion to make, and he covers it with the remark that under section 196 we are imposing additional burdens upon the farmers, and we may, therefore, reasonably and fairly, as a set-off against that, impose some further obligation with respect to these crossings upon the railway company. I am not saying whether or not the committee ought to require them to erect these cross fences. I have this observation to make with regard to the hon. gentleman's suggestion, that I do not see we are imposing any additional obligation, or one that involves a big charge upon the farmer in the clause that we have proposed.
In the crossing of live stock the same shall be in charge of some competent person who shall use all reasonable care and precaution to avoid accidents.
We provide that a person taking the live stock across a railway shall do what every careful man does do now, who is taking cattle across a railway over which perhaps many trains are running. Every person puts his cattle in the charge of competent hands, and he would be certain to have a suitable person in charge of the cattle. Therefore I cannot see that in the language of this clause we are making an undue demand upon the farmers or increasing their responsibility in the premises. Now, coming to the question of expense, I would be glad to have a more general expression of opinion from the committee as to the desirability of having this provision made. I confess that there is only one reason which can be assigned against adopting it, and that is, the one of expense. There are reasons which suggest themselves to my mind, and which have already been mentioned by the hon. member, why a precaution of this sort would be wise. But when we consider the number of crossings on these railroads already, the question whether the charge might not be unduly burdensome, is one that I would like to see more fully discussed by gentlemen who are better acquainted with the practical side oi; the question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am free to admit that it would be better to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Lincoln than to make no provision at all regarding the crossings ; but I am not free to admit that his is a better provision than the amendment I proposed myself. In the first place the proposition of the member for Lincoln would imply that at certain seasons of the year there would be along the ],ine of railway merely a number of boxes that would be filled up with snow, to the detriment of the
farmers who were passing to and fro, and it would not be found as workable. But my own proposition to make a permanent crossing beneath the railway
Would that fill up ?

It might fill up with snow, but it would be easier to remove it, because it would be on a lev'el track. But at the same time, you would have one under crossing where you woidd not have any over crossing. I will also admit the contention of the minister that it puts on the railway a considerable burden to provide for an under crossing. Whether we should impose that burden on the railway is not for me to say. At the present time I am asking for better protection for farmers and for their stock than they have in the provisions of the present Act. I realize that to require the company to make a crossing every few hundred yeards would perhaps be a burdensome thing for them to do, but in the long run, I think it would be to the advantage of the railway as well as to the farmers, because if they were maintained, they would be there for all time and would be a great convenience to the farmers.

I would like to mention to the minister one reason why 1 think, these under crossings would be objectionable. For instance, in the case where a farmer has part of his land on one side of the railway and a part on the other side, and is obliged to draw his hay across to his barn on the other side. In that case he would have to have two crossings, that is, an under crossing for cattle and an over crossing for his wagon. In other words, it would necessitate the railway giving that farmer a double crossing, unless the under crossing was made wide enough and deep enough to allow a load of hay passing through, It would be very costly to make the under crossing large enough for a load of hay or grain to pass. For this reason I think it would be a hardship to compel the railway to make an underneath crossing. Now, I have not heard of any complaint with regard to accidents at the crossings we now have, though of course there may be accidents now and then. But the great difficulty I have heard of among farmers is where the farm has been divided, where a farmer has sold off, say, fifty acres of his land. In a case of that kind this clause simply states that the farmer shall have a crossing. As long as the board would have a right to authorize the railway to grant a crossing in a case where they thought it was right, I think that is all that is required. So far as this amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln is qpncerned, I doubt myself whether it is really necessary. Of course cattle may go into a place that is fenced in, then turn around and run along the track, and it would be a great

difficulty to get tliem back. But I think, as a rule, cattle go straight across the track. However, I have not made any inquiries to ascertain whether such a change is necessary, hut I do not feel at present that it is necessary to impose such a burden on the railways.

I forgot to tell the minister a moment ago that a good many farmers have asked me if there was no way by which the Railway Committee of the Privy Council would permit them to go upon the railway lands and build these fences themselves. The farmers would he willing, if the railways would permit them, to go to the expense of digging these post holes and putting in the posts and putting on the boards or wires. The farmers will be willing, if the railways will permit them to go to the expense of digging these post holes and putting the necessary boards up, to do so, but I have been obliged to tell them that they Cannot go upon the railway lands and that I do not know any way in which they can get permission to do so.

When the hou. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) speaks of farmers one would suppose that he was representing all the farmers. I chance to represent a constituency composed largely of farmers, and I think it is my duty to speak for them. I assume that the hon. gentleman means to convey to the committee the impression that he speaks only for the farmers in his riding.
For the farmers generally in Ontario.

I do not know if he can speak for the farmers of Ontario, but certainly he cannot speak for the farmers outside of Ontario. As to the suggestion which has been made in regard to underground crossings or subway crossings I think that is not practicable at all. If they had these crossings dug underneath the railway during the winter time they would fill up with snow and in the spring and autumn they would fill up with water, and it would be impossible to drain them. I cannot see why there should be a demand for anything of that sort. The farmers are not a skim; for it.
They are asking for it.

The farmers would not ask for any such crossing as that, because I think it would be unreasonable and I do not like to hear it said that they are asking for anything unreasonable, because I have found the farmers to be intelligent men who are only asking for what is right. They are quick to ask for what is right and to obtain it too if they can. In regard to the other proposition made by the hon. member for Lincoln, I would be slow to take any suggestion of that sort until I had an opportunity of laying it before my constituents 195
who are largely made up of farmers. No complaint of that sort has come before me. The only demand that has come before me is for good substantial crossings, good gates with fastenings upon them and the only complaint is in regard to the matter of fires. This has been remedied in the Bill as it stands now. I can see very substantial objection to this proposal of fencing and there may be objections to it which would occur to the minds of farmers but would not occur to my mind and would not occur to the minds of very many of the hon. gentlemen present. If two lines of fences were built up to the track as has been suggested by one of the speakers, wlrat would be the result ? Suppose a man was driving a herd of cattle through from one side of the track, when the cattle come upon the track the most natural thing for them to do is to spread off each way. Before the farmer can bring them back he has to climb a four and a half foot fence, and if he is not more sprightly than some of us it will take him so long getting over the fence that the cattle will be away up the track and perhaps meet a locomotive before he overtakes them.

I do not think that would alarm the practical farmer.
Mi'. AVADE. AVhat does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) say ?
If the hon. gentleman does not know more about law than he does about farming, then he does not know anything about it and his opinion is not worth anything.

That is an expression of opinion by an hon. gentleman whose opinions do not meet with very much favour in this House. I think I know a great deal more about farming than the hon. gentleman does. I was brought up on a farm.
' Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit, there is more hope of a fool than of him.'

Satan quoting scripture. I usually know what I am talking about and that is the difference between the hon. gentleman and myself. One of these days I may be able to convince him that I do know something about law, but this House is not interested at the present moment in knowing whether I know anything about law or not. I would be very slow in asking this House to make any radical change in the Act affecting farmers until I had some complaint from the farmers I represent and until I know whether the proposed change will meet with their approval or not. This matter of fencing, this question of cattleguards and all these things have been before this House year aftei year. This is a new suggestion thrown out and I think the remarks of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals are very appropriate and pertinent when he says* that we

should take time to consider this matter before we make any change of this kind. I can see a further objection to the building of these fences. They would be a snow trap in winter time. The space between the two fences close together would fill up and blockade the crossing which would be a detriment to the farmer who has to use any of these crossings in the winter time. 1 do not believe there would be the slightest complaint on the part of the farmers as 'to farm crossings if all the gates were provided with proper fastenings and hinges so that they could be easily opened and closed.

I wish to say a word or two more in regard to the necessity of more crossings than one to each 100 acres. I understood the hon. minister to say that he had intended to direct his attention to this with a view of presenting an amendment. It was in that sense that I understood he had an amendment to propose, but he tells me now that he has no amend' ment.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the amendment I referred to and it is an amendment that would meet the case. If land changes hands there must be an owner of it and if the landowner is entitled to a crossing the board is empowered to order that it shall be provided. I am quite sure that it would be reasonable enough to do so, and therefore I think that would meet every requirement of the case so far a-s my judgment goes. That is the amendment I referred to, but I understood that the hon. minister was not prepared to make any amendment whatever.
I had in my mind that the hon. gentleman took the ground that the railway company should provide a crossing in respect to every other piece of land which had been cut-off from the larger portion,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: and which had passed into new hands, that wherever a farm was cut up the person who got the other portion of the land from the original owner would be entitled to a crossing. I thought that was what the hon. gentleman was asking for. I am very glad to hear that this will be satisfactory to him.

I have in my mind a case like this :	In our country the land
was originally laid out in fifty acre lots. One fifty acre lot was a free grant and the adjoining one was what would be called in the North-west a pre-emption lot. The settlers might retain that pre-emption lot or drop it, or sell his right to some other person after he had improved his own lot and increased its value. He might sell his right to that fifty acres to some other person. The farm was originally 100 acres aud the railway crossed the 100 acres and gave but one crossing. It was to meet such a case as that that I wished to have the clause amended, but I think this will meet the case in every respect, and I am satisfied with it. As to having crossings underneath the railway I can readily understand that it would be convenient for the farmers, but the objection is raised that it would tend to interfere with the safety of the travelling public, and it would also be enormously expensive as it would mean a subway about every quarter mile. I think the House will feel reluctant to order such a thing as that. These subways would also be troublesome inasmuch as they would be likely to fill up with snow. The hon. gentleman from Annapolis said that the fences would also pile up snow in winter, but if they are wire fences there would be no danger from that source. I confess that I do not look with very great favour upon the proposal to build these fences to the track, for unless there be a cattle-guard at every one of these crossings the cattle may frequently get on the track. It does seem to me that if the farmers have proper level crossings it is all you can reasonably expect the railways to provide. In the original clause it was stated that these crosssings should be for farm purposes, and I am glad the clause has ibeen amended with regard to that. I know a case where the person who purchased one portion of a sub-divided farm claimed the right to have a crossing and he allowed others to cross, but the company objected because he had only the right to cross himself and then only for farm purposes. This is an unnecessary and unjust restriction, and I am glad to see that the section has been amended so that the board may order a crossing on whatever terms they deem proper.

The minister intimated that he was willing to take sugestions from practical men, and I suppose he meant those who were accustomed to drive cattle across a railway track.
[DOT]6213

Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

In that respect I am practical, and I may tell the minister that while I do not want to make a speech for -* Hansard,' I will give him my view. As to the member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) I will dispose of him by quoting a passage from Scripture ;
Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit there is more hope of a fcol than of him.
Hear, hear.

As to fencing the crossings, the arguments made by some hon. members are fallacious. When the person in charge of the cattle opens the gate and the cattle go through, the first thing that attracts their attention is the long grass on both sides of the railway track, and their instinct is to scatter in different directions to get at that grass, and if a train comes along an accident may happen. If there were wire fences running along each side of the crossing, then nothing but the bare track would be open to the cattle and the chances are ten to one that they will not go on the bare track. I would not require those fences to be as high as the farm fences, but if there *was some kind of a fence running up to the track which would prevent the cattle from turning to the right or to the left it would be a great improvement on the existing condition of things. As to tunnel crossings no matter how convenient they might be to the farmers I would not vote for it because of the extremely detrimental effect that it is bound to have on the operation of railways. However, now that we are legislating to make the farmers cautious we should also make the railways a little more cautious to protect the farmers, and if the minister would carry out the suggestions which I make it would have a tendency in that direction.
Hear, hear.

I was glad to hear the minister invite suggestions from practical men and I shall avail myself of that invitation. I take it that the railways formerly construed the existing law to mean that they must keep up fences on those crossings because along the Grand Trunk Railway and the Toronto Hamilton and Buffalo there were originally fences at all these crossings. I cannot imagine it possible that such a Bill as this should go through parliament without providing for these fences. If the existing law does not provide for them, then a clause such as that proposed by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) should be inserted. One man could not tend a drove of cattle crossing the track; It would require two or three men. It is a very easy matter to maintain light fences of wire which would not catch the snow, and I believe that all the railway companies of this country feel the necessity of build-1954
ing these fences; but when we are passing the Railway Bill we might as well make it clear. A word with regard to underground crossings. Originally there were underground crossings under the Grand Trunk Railway, and that I suppose was one reason why it cost $100,000 a mile. Now, since the wooden crossings have rotted away, the company are putting in expensive stone crossings, being obliged by the terms of their agreement with the farmers to do so; but they are making them so narrow that they are practically of no use. There has been some litigation with regard to them, but as a rule the farmers dread the expense of litigation with a railway company. Some of the crossings which were originally ten feet wide have been reduced to three or four feet, which will not let more than one animal go through at a time. The danger to the railway of these crossings is so great that I could not consent to vote that they should be built. One objection has been urged to them is that they get filled up with snow. This objection is quite invalid because farmers do not pasture their cattle in the winter time, consequently do not care whether they fill up with snow or not. But I think it is absolutely essential that provision should be made that these fences should be built at every farm crossing, unless this is done I feel sure there will be a great outcry among the farming community and I think justly so.

I do not think I would have said anything on this clause had I not been specially referred to by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). Having been formerly connected with a railway company, it might appear that what I say might be influenced somewhat by that fact. However, for a good many years I have had no interest in nor connection with any railway company. At the same time, I have had a good many years' experience on many of the questions that have been discussed here; and I can say, after hearing what has been said, that there is a good deal of truth and a good deal of error on all sides. The hon. member for Huron has referred to an agreement which he says was drawn up by me some twenty or twenty-five years ago. I have no doubt whatever that the agreement he refers to, if it exists, was drawn by me. In the case hf the railway to which he alludes, all agreements that were entered into were put In writing; and I can only say that from my long experience of railway companies, I do not believe that either the Grand Trunk, 'which now owns the road which he referred to, or any other railway in this country, would repudiate a written agreement which had been entered into by the company or by its predecessor. I have never yet known an agreement to be repudiated in that way, and I think there must be some mistake. I can only say that if the Grand Trunk Company is repudiating such an agreement,

'I should -be happy to assist to the utmost of my power in compelling the company to adhere to that agreement to the last letter. I can hardly believe that a railway company would be guilty of such dishonourable conduct as to repudiate such an agreement. With regard to the point the hon. gentleman makes as to underground crossings, I know that the railway companies of this country have spent thousands of dollars in buying up these crossings in the interest of the safety of trains that run over their tracks. Every person connected with railways knows that every hole in the track is an element of danger. If a wheel gets off the track and runs along an embankment, there is frequently no serious accident; tout if a "wheel runs off the track and gets into one of these underground crossings, there may toe a very serious catastrophe involving loss of life. There have been many devices to get over the difficulty; but the railway companies, in the interest of their passengers, in the interest of their men, and in the interest of the safety of their rolling stock, have spent many thousands of dollars in buying up these crossings. I think the safety of the trains is the great consideration that should be given weight to here, and I should be very sorry if this parliament should under any circumstances commit itself to ordering the construction of underground farm crossings. With regard to the cross fences, I think most hon. gentlemen will recollect that some ten or fifteen years ago, along the railways in the province of Ontario there were to be seen many fence posts which had formerly been fences at farm crossings; but if the hon. gentleman could travel along all the railways of Ontario to-day he would see very few of these cross fences existing. It has been said here to-night that it is all nonsense to say that the farmers object to them. I know personally that many farmers have objected; they have told me that they do not want them. If the farmers thought they "were good, they would have been continued; but many who had agreements with the railway companies requiring these fences abandoned them and have not insisted on the agreement to keep them up. The reason is obvious enough. Cattle will get on to the railway whether driven across it or not. Farm servants, children, and others, "will be negligent, and will leave gates open; colts and cattle will get out and ramble along the track; the train will come along, the animal will run ahead of the train until It comes to the cross fence when it will run "up to the opening and get killed. It is an element of danger. Formerly, when the fences were of wood, there was another element of danger in these cross fences, the danger of fire with the train rushing along and the sparks flying backwards, these fences were liable to catch fire and conduct the fire into the farms. But it seems to me there is not much in the point, because under the clause proposed by the minister, if the board should come to the conclusion that these fences are necessary or expedient, it can order them. The language of the clause permits the board to order any kind of crossing they like. It says they may order and direct how, when, where, by whom and upon what terms and conditions such farm crossing shall be constructed and maintained. These terms are broad enough to enable the board to order any kind of fence that may be required at a crossing. With regard to public crossings, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has said that the minister proposes to add some wofdis here which impose a greater burden on the farmer or the person living in the neighbourhood of the crossing than has hitherto existed. There is not one word in this clause that any judge of the land would not say is part of the law as it stands today. Every lawyer knows that a judge, in directing a jury on this subject, would say that the law providing that the cattle or horses should be in charge of some person does not mean merely that the person may be there without doing anything. Over and over again it has been decided that if the person in charge did not take reasonable care to protect the cattle in crossing, the complainant had no case. All that; the minister has done is to add words wHich make the legal effect clear to the ordinary lay mind, and it is better that the farmer should know exactly what the law means than have to go to a lawyer to interpret it.

I do not think that the hon. gentleman could have considered the language preceding this. There is not a word in the provision of the law preceding this, requiring that any one must be in charge of the stock. There is a great difference between having to be guided by the common law as regards what is contributory negligence and making a special enactment saying that a certain thing must be done. In the latter case if that thing be not done there is of course negligence, whereas, under the common law, all the circumstances being considered, there might not be negligence.

While I do not think we would be justified in passing legislation to compel railway companies to construct under crossings, still I do think that some provision should be made compelling the railway companies to give the farmers the use of existing structures where they may be of service. I have an instance in my mind of a culvert which is sufficiently large to allow cattle to pass through it. The farmer has land on both sides of this culvert, and during the greater part of the summer the watercourse is dry and cattle could pass through without any injury. The farmer would be willing to put the necessary side

fences from the division fence to the culvert, and if necessary to plank the bottom of the culvert, so that the cattle could pass through without tramping up the bottom. It would not put the railway to any additional expense if he were allowed to use this culvert, and I think that a provision might he inserted compelling the railway companies in such cases to allow the use of their structures for the passage of cattle.

If the hon. minister considers he will be imposing too great a burden on the railway companies to compel them to make these double fences, he should at least give the farmers the right to build them themselves if they consider them of advantage. I know where farmers have built fences from the railway lence to as near the railway track as possible in order to get cattle over with less trouble. One man could handle a dozen cattle easier where there is a fence on each side up to that track than two men could where there is no such fence. The fact that the municipalities compel the railway companies to put fences up at the highways is proof that the people believe it is easier to get cattle to pass between a fourteen or fifteen feet gap than through one of two rods. The railway companies should either be compelled to put these fences up themselves or allow the farmers to put them up if they require them.

Does the hon. member for South Perth say that the railway companies object to their culverts being used for the passage of cattle, when they are in such a condition that they may be used for that purpose V

1 know that an owner of property told me a few days ago that he would like to see some provision made which would give him the right to make use of a railway culvert by building all the necessary works himself. Whether he applied to the company and was refused, I am not in a position to say.

In that case there is nothing in the contention of the hon. gentleman. We know that in the last twenty-five years the construction and operation of railways have undergone a great change. The reason why underground crossings have been done away with is because the companies have changed very materially their system of operating. Years ago their rolling stock was much lighter but when they concluded to make their rolling stock heavier, when they decided to increase their engine power, they found that it was necessary to close up these under crossings because they interfered with the solidity of the road-bed. The first thing to be considered is the safety of the travelling public, and it was that which the railway companies had in view when they filled up these under ground crossings. Then we have water passing under the railways in many {daces. Formerly many railways had wooden bridges over these water courses, whereas to-day they have very strong structures built over them in order to make them perfectly safe and strengthen the road-bed. I did attend meetings of the Gattle-guard Commission, and I found farmers stating that they did not attach as much importance to the cattle guards as.they did to farm crossings and the way they were kept on different railways. They say that they used the private farm crossings fifty times for once they used a highway crossing. The principal reason for using the farm crossing was to drive their stock and produce back and forth, and they thought some steps should !be taken in order to protect their stock and loads of produce going over the track from time to time. And they suggested that fences be run from the gate near to the rails on the railway. I am not prepared to say that that would be a good thing. I do not know from j)ersonal experience whether it would be or not. But perhaps I might be permitted to suggest an idea in view of what the farmers stated. They said they would be willing to furnish the material and do the work themselves, if the railway companies would give permission sooner than do without them. Under this section the board would be empowered to consider the applications ot these people :	and, where there would
be no harm in allowing a wire fence from the farm crossing gate up to the railway, if the farmer chooses to provide such a fence, I do not see any reason why the board should not have the power to allow the farmers to brake the fence. That seems to be the idea ol these farmers, rightly or wrongly. Having been present and having heard their views, I think it is my duty to lay those views before this committee. So far as authority for creating these farm crossings are concerned, I think the amendment proposed by the hon. minister will cover the point.
The remarks made do not apply to the case I referred to. The culvert is an open culvert and the cattle, if permitted to pass through it, would not add at all to the danger of running trains.
What railway 1
The Grand Trunk Railway.

I believe that if the right were granted to farmers to make the fences from the farm gate up to near the rails it would facilitate the crossing of cattle and would also, to a large extent, provide for the case mentioned by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). And I think that the farmer should be allowed to make these fences .if he thinks it best to do so in his own interest. It would be no disadvantage to the railway whatever. It would be better to have wire fences, as they would not catch the snow.

In view of the great difference of opinion of the committee as to the possibility of adding a clause requiring these fences to lie constructed at farm crossings, I think it would be unwise to adopt the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). But it will be observed that the board is fully empowered to deal with this question. The board can inform themselves as to the utility and desirability of having these fences, and they can require the railway companies to construct them if they think it well to do so. I think the matter stands in very good shape as it is, and that it would be undesirable to adopt the amendment. My hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Erb) has expressed the wish that, if possible, a clause may be included in the Act enabling farmers to utilize the culverts or arches which are on their farms-, for the purpose of driving cattle through. I apprehend there cannot be many cases of that kind, and that this is not a matter requiring provision in a general law of this kind. At this time it could not be satisfactorily dealt with. Not having heard of it before, I am not in a position to pass on it satisfactorily. I think my hon. friend will see the desirability of not asking me to make an amendment of that kind at present.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would there be any objection to empowering the commission to deal with these applications if they are made ?
Would not the board have power to deal with it under the subsection proposed by the hon. minister ?
I think under the general powers it might.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That would answer.

Referring to the suggestion of the hon. minister that there would not be much harm in leaving this question of fences between the farm gate and the railway to the board, I would point out that the board will probably be guided in their decisions by what they find in the law. In ordering a new farm crossing, they would naturally say : We should not provide that these fences shall be made, because other farm crossings have not these fences. If we are of opinion that these fences ought to be made, we ought to say so in' the statute.
I remarked that in view of the great difference of opinion on the part of the committee, we should not make the provision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think there is a strong majority in favour.
I doubt it. I think the strength of the argument may be said to be against
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: the hon. member's amendment. I think the general power given to the board to require any appliances that they think necessary at crossings, will apply to these farm crossings and the protection of them. If there is a case made out in favour of placing these fences on each side of the farm gate, there is no doubt but the board has power and it would act upon that power.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are a number of amendments to be dealt with. They are all amendments' to the clause, and not to other amendments. The first is that of Mr. Cowan

In order to clear the atmosphere, I may say that when I moved the amendment the other day to clause 196, the clause stood as printed in the original Bill, and no subsection was proposed, so far as I knew. But subsection 2, as now proposed, obviates the necessity for the amendment I proposed. Therefore, with the consent of the seconder (Mr. Thompson, Haldi-mand), I beg leave to withdraw the amendment I made.
Amendment (Mr. Cowan) withdrawn.
Amendment (Mr. Holmes) negatived.
Amendment (Mr. Lancaster) negatived.
Amendment (Hon. Mr. Blair) agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 197-fences, cattle-guards.
I think section 197 should be dealt with in connection with section 237. Now in connection with this cattle-guard question-
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a word ?
No, I will not.
I merely wanted to say

I have the floor at the present time. I am not in the habit of wasting the time of the House. While we on this side of the House have been paying just as much attention, and perhaps more attention, to this Bill than hon. gentlemen opposite have been doing, they have been trying to create the impression in the country that they are the only people who are paying any attention to this Bill at all. I want to say in the first place that the people of this country will view with a great deal of satisfaction the conduct of the minister who has charge of this Bill, in the first place, for the great care, consideration and judgment he has manifested in its preparation ; in the next place, for the calm and judicial way in which he has presented the Bill before the House, and the readiness with which he has invited criticism from both sides, and has yielded to all sorts of suggestions for the purpose 1 of perfecting this Bill. I believe that the

Bill will become law one of these days, and that it will reflect the greatest possible credit on the lion. Minister of Railways. Now there has been a great difference of opinion as to what form an amendment in respect to cattle-guards should take to remedy the evil which certainly exists, to the detriment of the farmers and owners of cattle. That fact is very apparent from what occurred last year. A number of gentlemen have sought to frame an amendment to the existing law which will be generally satisfactory. There is no question that while this matter of cattle-guards is important to every province of Canada, it is especially important to the province of Ontario, and the farmers of that province have taken more interest in it than the farmers of any other part of the Dominion. Last year there were several amendments proposed to the existing legislation in respect to cattle-guards. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) proposed an amendment, and when we came to consider it we found that the phraseology of that amendment was defective, perhaps from the reason indicated to-night by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) who, in speaking on another section, said in effect that it was desirable that changes made in the legislation should be in such a form that farmers and ordinary men who are not accustomed, like lawyers, to examining legal phraseology, should be able to understand exactly what the statute meant. Now, whether it was the ambiguous terms of the amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln or for some other reason, there has been a great deal of difficulty in ascertaining the exact meaning of that amendment, and a difference of opinion as to whether it remedies the evil which we are all seeking to remedy. In dealing with this question we must not treat it as a party question, we must find the phraseology that will accomplish the purpose that we have in view. Our purpose is to place the onus in the right quarter. Hitherto the result of litigation has been almost invariably that the farmer found himself out of court. Now what we want to do by this legislation is to place the onus upon the railway company when cattle are killed or injured. Without debating this question at great length, because it has been threshed out over and over again, I propose to offer an amendment which, to some extent, embodies much of the phraseology which the Minister of Railways, after a great deal of pains and attention, has suggested. While I have used to some extent the careful and exact phraseology of the Minister of Railways, still I do not think it goes to the root of the matter, or goes as far as the farmers desire and is necessary. I have gone a little farther, and I propose to read to the committee the amendment which I suggest, and in which I think all will concur. My amendment which I move as a subsection to section 197, reads as follows :
When any cattle or other animals at large upon the highway or otherwise, get upon the property of the company and are killed or Injured by a train, the owner of such animals so killed or injured shall be entitled to recover the amount of such loss or injury against the company in any action in any court of competent jurisdiction, unless the company in the opinion of the court or jury trying the case establishes that such animal got at large through negligence or wilful neglect or omission of the owner or his agent, or of the custodian of such animal or his agent ; hut the fact that such animal was not in charge of some competent person or persons shall not for the purpose of this subsection, deprive the owner of his right to recover.
I submit that is a good clear cut amendment which both sides can concur in, and which will exactly meet the situation.

That would more properly be moved as subsection 4 to section 237. I wish to move an amendment such as I have handed to you, Mr. Chairman. I beg to move :
That subsection three of section 237, line three, be amended by inserting after the word ' train ' the words ' at such point of intersection,' and to add as subsection four the following :
4. Whenever any cattle, at large upon the highway or otherwise, get upon the property of the company and are killed or injured by a train, the owner of such cattle so killed or injured. shall be entitled to recover the amount of such loss or injury against the company in an action in any court of competent jurisdiction, if in the opinion of the judge, who tries the action, such cattle got at large without any negligent or wilful act or omission of the owner or his agent, or of the custodian of such cattle or his agent, and got upon the railway by reason of fences, gates and cattle-guards not being erected and maintained by the company as required by this Act.
I move this as an amendment which has commended itself to my mind after giving the subject a good deal of consideration and with every desire to go as far as I think parliament can properly go in meeting the wishes and demands of the people who are interested in this question. I am well aware that the feeling is extremely strong, more particularly in sections of the province of Ontario. It seems to me further that the question is one of a character that might fairly be regarded as an open question in the House and as one upon which hon. members on both sides might very fairly vote according to their judgment with regard to the consideration that the Bill in which this section is being embodied Is a government Bill. I would think, that, probably, under existing circumstances, having regard to the differences of opinion and to the different judgments, because men will differ upon the same facts, of hon. members, it would be fair to all parties that they should vote lipj*n the different principles that are sub-rnitted in regard to this Bill ns open questions. My objection to the motion which the

lion, member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) has moved is that I think it imposes too great a responsibility upon the railway company when it insists that the railway company shall establish negligence on the part of the owner of the cattle. We had a case which was dealt with yesterday in which we placed the onus upon the railway company of showing that where fire occurred the equipment of the locomotive was such as was required by law and that the fire had been caused through no defect in the apparatus used for the purpose of preventing fires. We imposed that obligation upon the railway company of rebutting and showing that it was not guilty of negligence. In a case like the present one, dealing with all interests and all parties fairly, it appears to me that it is unjust to ask that the railway company shall give evidence or actual proof that the farmer was guilty of negligence in allowing his cattle to run unattended when it must be physically and morally and actually impossible that the railway company can have any knowledge upon the question. The owner of the cattle, or the persons in charge of the cattle, are the only persons who can know whether or not they have been negligent and it is easy for them to show that they have not been negligent and in showing that they .have not been negligent they will he entitled to recover. Under the other clause they might recover although they had been negligent and although they were not in justice entitled to recover, because the railway company might fail to establish the actual facts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am surprised a little that the hon. gentleman for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) so poorly bears out the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that we heard last night to the effect that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have not assisted in improving this Bill, but, that hon. gentlemen on Ids own side of the House by going to him privately had been able to do a great deal in assisting him to amend this Bill. At the time the hon. gentleman made that statement it struck me that if it had not been for the opposition very few amendments would have been made to this Bill in favour of the people. All the amendments which have been made to this Bill in favour of the people have emanated from this side of the House. When the hon. minister said that amendments had been made at the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite it struck me that he must have been referring to- amendments in favour of the railways, and I think the hon. member for North Essex has proved 1 was right about that, because, notwithstanding the assertion of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals yesterday and notwithstanding the assertion of the hon. member for North Essex, we find that the hon. member for North Essex lias to come here to-night and invoke the aid of members of Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
the opposition in order to compel the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to do what a humble member of the opposition for three sessions lias been trying to compel him to do. The member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) knew that unless lie got the assistance of the opposition in this House who are sincere in the matter, he could not prevail on the Minister of Railways and Canals to make the amendment. I may say at the outset that I will support the amendment.
Hear, hear.

I do not believe in treating these gentlemen opposite in the same spirit as they have treated me. For three sessions I have urged this matter on the attention of parliament, but I have obtained no support from the minister or from the member for North Essex. I hope that the next time the hon. minister and the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) believe in the justice of a proposition which emanates from this side of the House, they will not wait for three long years to do what is right in the interest of the farmers of this country. Now, I am generous enough to congratulate the member for North Essex for coming to our relief, if he wants to put it that way, and assisting us to put into force a law which the majority on this side of the House have been urging for the last three years. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there is not a particle of difference in the legal effect of the amendment which he has introduced and the one which I have been introducing for the last three sessions. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) knows that full well, but I want to bring another matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals and of the House, which requires amendment, and I think all will agree that it is a thing which does require amendment. Let me first tell the hon. member for North Essex that he need not have been afraid, when he refused to let me say a few words, he having the floor, he need not have heen afraid that I was going to steal his thunder. I had not the remotest idea of moving an amendment different to his when I rose in my place and I had no idea of depriving him of the kudos of moving his amendment. I am not looking for that kind of cheap glory that some members on the other side of the House may be looking for, and may think I am looking for. Since I was elected to serve the people of the electoral district of Lincoln and Niagara I have endeavoured to do my duty an'd it matters not to me from what source legislation may come, if it be in the interest of the people I shall support it. I have no doubt that if I had moved an amendment exactly the same as he has moved he would feel it his duty to his party to oppose it acting on his record, but I am not made of that kind of stuff and therefore I will be glad that we on tills side of the House have been

able to convince the minister and his supporters that this long standing grievance of the farmers ought be remedied now. But the bon. member for North Essex has not provided an effectual cure, and it will therefore be necessary to move an amendment in regard to section 237. When the proper time comes I shall move to strike out the words ' or straying upon the railway ' in the last line of that section. The hon. member for North Essex in his hurry to prepare his amendment has not looked' into the whole law carefully. If he paid one-tenth as much attention to this matter as some members on this side have, he would have discovered for himself if the Minister of Railways did not tell him, that there are a few words in section 237 which seriously interfere with the good effect of his amendment. The Minister of Railways and Canals promised to remedy the grievances of the farmers in this respect last session, but he kept that pledge the same as he and his government have been keeping other pledges since 189G. He puts in section 237 a provision that a farmer must have sufficient help to keep the animals from straying on the railway tracks, and now, in view of this amendment he tries to make the farmer be a cattle-guard himself. When he first introduced this Bill into the House instead of remedying the grievances of the farmers, you will be surprised to hear that he not only compelled the farmer to have control of the animals at the point of intersection and to see them safely across the track, but he added the words that the farmer shall have sufficient help to prevent the animals from straying upon the railway. Now, this is an additional burden on the farmers. What are the cattle-guards there for if not to stop the animals from straying on the railway. I am bound to tell the hon. member for North Essex that in order to make this legislation workable he must help me to strike out these words ' from straying upon the railway ' so that the Act will not be inconsistent, and so that judges may not disagree as to what these two sections mean when you take them together. We must have some language in this Act which will be understood by the farmers and which they will not have to get lawyers to construe for them. The hon. member for North Essex has not been able to see that this section has to be amended in order to make his amendment workable. Because of the want of his eye-glasses or for some other reason he has overlooked the fact that these words still remain in the Bill, placing an additional burden on the farmer and compelling him to have enough people at the point of intersection to prevent the animals from straying on the railway, notwithstanding that cattle-guards are there for that purpose. We have had already three amendments proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals trying to get this cattle-guard legislation in proper shape, and at last, after deep consultation between the farmers from North Essex and .the Minister of Railways and Canals we have this fourth drawn section which I am glad to say is the best of the lot, and which I think will be supported on this side of the House. What the Minister of Railways and Canals has done up to date is to endeavour to impose additional burdens upon the farmers instead of remedying their acknowledged grievances, but now he seems to be on the right track and for my part I am disposed to help him out and to make his ideas workable. In the first place I want the Minister of Railways and Canals to tell us why he added these words ' or straying upon the railway.' Why does he come to this House and state that he is giving cattle-guards that will be suitable and sufficient and at the same time provide that the farmer who heretofore had to prevent the animals from loitering at the point of intersection, has now to prevent them from straying upon the railway while the cattle-guards are there to prevent them from straying, if the law he is introducing is of any good ? I could understand it if the hon. minister has been assisted by the railway lawyers in drawing this section; because they want a conflict of sections. The railway companies are interested in having laws passed which are not easy to understand, and about which the courts will disagree. The farmer cannot afford to go to law with the railway companies on doubtful matters if he expects to have any part of his farm left. The railway companies like to have laws which are doubtful in meaning, which will result in lawsuits, and the Minister of Railways and Canals has added clauses here which will make this law inconsistent with itself, so that if a farmer goes to court and sues the railway company for the loss of an animal as a result of the absence of these cattle-guards, the judge will be obliged to say to the plaintiff's counsel, it is a grave question whether you or the railway company is most to blame, because at the same session and in the same Railway Bill that is supposed to give the remedy, an amendment has been inserted at the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals which makes the remedy doubtful.
I understand that the hon. gentleman argues that the amendment of the hon. member for North Essex is a little inconsistent with section 237 ?

The hon. member for North Essex has moved as an amendment a separate clause, and the clause before this House contains these words, ' or straying on the railway ' which were not in the law until this session, but which are now being put in by the Minister of Railways.
I do not just understand wherein the Inconsistency lies, from listening to the hon. member.

He has not got to that point yet.

speechtext: That means that the Minister of Railways does not understand it either. And as the hon. member for South Essex is so very fond of interrupting every body, if he still says lie cannot understand me, I cannot help it; the fault must be with his own intelligence.
