I am satisfied that the Minister of Railways knows what i mean, and that he must have had some reason for putting in these words ' or straying on the railway.' They never were there until this year.
I am not rising for the purpose of interrupting. I just wish to ask a question.
I think the hon. member is rising just to bother me. If he wants to ask me any question, I am willing to be cross-examined, if it will do him any good.

I do not want to crossexamine. I simply rise because I do not grasp the point the hon. gentleman is making. I would be glad if he would make it clear wherein there is inconsistency between the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Essex and section 237 ?

If the hon. member will listen, I will endeavour to tell him ; but if he insists on talking to himself and jumping up like a jack-in-the-box, I do not suppose I can make him understand it. The hon. member for North Essex lias introduced an amendment which puts a liability on the railway to pay for the animal notwithstanding that no human being was in control of it, if it gets on the track and is killed by the railway. The section, as the Minister of Railways has amended it-and this is a new law, added by the Minister of Railways this year-provides that the farmer must not only have enough competent people to prevent the animal loiteriug at the point of intersection, but even from straying on the railway. If the hon. member for South Essex was a judge, who would he say was entitled to recover under these circumstances ?

The hon. member for Lincoln has asked me a question. What I would like to do is to read the few last lines of the amendment of the hon. member for North Essex
But the fact that such animal was not in charge of some competent person or persons, shall not. for the purpose of this subsection, deprive the owner of his right to recover.

The hon. member for South Essex asked me wherein the amendment of the hon. member for North Essex was inconsistent with section 237. The Min-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
ister of Railways has added words which require that the farmer must not only have sufficient help to prevent the animals loitering at the point of intersection, but even from going on the railway, which is the very thing the cattle-guards are intended to stop. So that if you have accidents, which both the hon. member for North Essex and I are trying to prevent, unless you strike out these words ' or straying on the railway,' you are making a nonsensical law which can be read one minute in favour of the farmer and the next minute in favour of the railway company. Both parties will be in fault, both will have contributed, and the complainant Will not be able to recover. The farmer will have to be the complainant. He cannot stop the train from running and make the railway company sue. The train keeps on killing the cattle and the farmer is to blame if he did not have sufficient help to stop the animal from going on the railway, and the railway is to blame for not having cattle-guards. We must be sensible, and I am glad that the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) is at last in the frame of mind to accept sensible legislation, and I submit to him my amendment, hoping that he will accept it in the spirit in which I accepted his, and let the farmers have their grievances remedied, no matter Who gets the credit.

The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) seems desirous to pick a quarrel with me because I would not make way for him after I had risen to move my amendment. Are we to understand that every time an hon. gentleman on this side or the other happens to rise to make a motion or to speak to some motion before the Chair, he must make way for the hon. member for Lincoln, if that hon. gentleman desires to speak ? This is the third time to-night that he has expressed his displeasure because he was not given precedence when he desired to address the House.
Talk to the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan).

I am addressing the hon. member who has just spoken, and I wish him to understand that when I rise and have the floor, I do not propose to give way even to so important a personage as the hon. member for Lincoln. I do not propose to allow myself to be sidetracked by him and resume my seat to suit his pleasure or convenience. In his desire to pose as a friend of the farmer, the hon. gentleman said that no amendment to this Bill had emanated from this side at all. Why, within the last couple of hours, one of the most important, perhaps the most important, that has yet come up was the amendment moved by my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Cowan).
I said before tonight.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken. He did not say before to-night, and ' Hansard ' will bear me out.
I certainly intended to say so, and 1 maintain that I did say so.

The great difficulty with the hon. member for Lincoln is this, that when he addresses the House he effervesces to such an extent that he scarcely knows what he is talking about. He undertook to say that I had suddenly discovered an interest in this Bill. Well, no one knows better than the hon. gentleman that last year I was watcUng this Bill very carefully and moved an amendment in the Railway Committee along the same lines as that which I moved to-night. Last year also I moved this amendment to his own measure :	^ Unless in the opinion of
the court or jury, the owner of such animals shall have been guilty of negligence, but no presumption of negligence shall arise by reason of the animal being unattended on the highway.' If the hon. member for Lincoln had received that amendment in the spirit in which he should have received it, we would have had that substantial measure of improvement made last year to the law, but he would not accept it. He was so anxious to get the measure through in the shape he wished that he would not accept any reasonable suggestion. I have been watching this Bill as closely as the hon. gentleman, and the fact that I moved a resolution last year similar to the one I have moved to-night is proof of this.
Does the hon. gentleman say that he moved that in the Railway Committee last year ?
That is what I said.
Was it voted on ?
It was.
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken.

My hon. friend is again wrong. My hon. friend from Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) whom I see in the House will remember that after he moved this amendment :	' Without any negligence or default on the part of the owner or person to whose care or keeping such animal has been entrusted.' I moved the amendment I have just read, and it was disposed of by the Railway Committee. The hon. gentleman further insinuated that I am a railway or corporation lawyer and am attempting to deal with this matter from that standpoint. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied that no corporation or railway will be very well pleased with my amendment, and it is quite as stringent as the amendment he has suggested and perhaps more so. But apparently the hon. gentleman-for the reason I gave a few minutes
ago, namely, that he gets too heated and excited-is unable to appreciate the force of the amendment I have suggested. It is perfectly clear that the latter part of the amendment quite obviates the difficulty Which the hon. gentleman sees in section 1 of this section which I am proposing to amend.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us whether he thinks that these words ' or straying upon a railway ' ought to be in subsection 1 ?
I think they are quite covered by my amendment.
Do they strengthen the hon. gentleman's amendment or weaken it ?
I do not think they affect it one way or the other.
The fact that the farmer himself now is bound to prevent the animals straying upon the railway does not affect the hon. gentleman's amendment ?
No. What I am providing is that the fact that the animals are not attended shall not take away the right of action from the farmer.

Will the hon. gentleman tell us whether he does not think that the very object he seeks to gain by his amendment would be better served by striking out those words ? Why should the farmer not only be bound to prevent the animals loitering at the point of intersection, but also prevent them from straying on the railway track ?

I am not dealing with that section in that sense at all. Whether that section stands with or without those words, the amendment I propose will cover it, and the hon. gentleman knows that to be the fact.
I know the very opposite might be argued.

As the hon. gentleman has favoured me with some choice flowers from his rhetorical conservatory, such as describing me as a Jack-in-the-box, besides showering on me like complimentary epithets, I shall try and enlighten him to a certain extent upon some matters in connection with this section which, I am sorry to say, the hon. member for Lincoln apparently does not understand. The section is one which I venture to say every hon. member of this House who has listened to the hon. member is convinced he does not understand. Before proceeding further, however, I wish to assure the hon. member for Lincoln that I entirely absolve him from any responsibility for my lack of comprehension to which he has referred. If he has brains to understand, he certainly has not given any evidence of it. Judging by his attempted argu-1 ment, he is not over blessed with that com-

rnodity, and I will go a step further and tell him that his ability to transmit what may be in his own mind to the minds of others has not been displayed at any time to any considerable extent. I therefore quite absolve the hon. member from any responsibility for the so-called arguments which he attempted to make and any lack of comprehension to which he has referred. Now, it seems to me that that subsection 1 of section 237 is quite clear. For the benefit of those members of the committee who have not the Railway Bill before them, I will read it:
No horses, sheep, swine or other cattle shall be permitted to be at large on any highway within half a mile of the intersection of such
highway with any railway at rail level-
-this is the old law, and a very proper one, for cattle have no business to be on the highway within half a mile of the highway, unless they are in charge of some competent person, or unless without the negligence of the owner they chance to be there

-unless such cattle are in charge of some competent person or persons, to prevent their loitering or stopping on such highway at such intersection, or straying upon the railway.
Now, the whole principle of the railway law is that cattle shall not be within half a mile of the railway unless they are in charge of some competent person. But there is an exception, and that exception is when without negligence and without fault of the owner of these cattle they are at large upon the highway within half a mile of the railway. In that event, there is no liability on the part of the railway. The hon. member for North Essex, following out this year the principles he enunciated last year, and which, I can tell the hon. member for Lincoln the hon. member for North Essex has enunciated and followed ever since he became a respected member of this House, moved this amendment and put in the express exception in order to meet just such cases as the hon. member for Lincoln's imagination led him to believe might arise. And that was, as I read it before-this is subsection 1 of section 237-but the fact that such cattle or other animals are not in charge of some competent person or persons shall not deprive the owner of his right of recovery. That is as plain as the English language can make it.
We all know that. Mr. COWAN. I am glad you know it.
I knew it before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) did.

If you had only let me tell you when you were on your feet, you would have known it now.
Mr. LANCASTER, I knew it twenty years ago.

I should have thought that the knowledge that the hon. gentleman has carried about with him for twenty years Mr. COWAN.	'	'
might have leaked out of him when he was trying to bestow some of his wisdom upon this House to-night. Now, this is the hon. member who says he knew this twenty years ago who now rises and says it is not true-
No, I did not.
You may not have intended it, and I was surprised when you did it-but you did it.
Address the Chair.
I beg the Chairman's pardon.	t

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It will take a certain sting out of the discussion if hon. members, when speaking, address the Chair.

I most humbly apologize, Mr. Chairman. I do not always follow the hon. member for Lincoln-in fact I rarely do-but under the influence of his example there are some bad habits which I naturally fall into. If the hon. member for Lincoln knew this twenty years ago, why not adopt it ? Why was it necessary for him to spend half an hour heaping abuse, or trying to heap abuse, upon the hon. member for North Essex, using the words as ' cheap glory ' in referring to the hon. gentleman's motives, simply because the hon. member for North Essex moved an amendment which the hon. member for Lincoln himself accepts, which he says is a fit and proper amendment. Yet, having accepted it, he says that the man who proposes it is simply trying to get cheap glory, leaving it to be inferred that he, the hon. member for Lincoln is the great hero struggling for the rights of the people. But, he says, any man who brings forward anything with which I agree, is a cheap glory man, but I am the man who is trying to secure the rights of the people. I want to say to the hon. member for Lincoln-and I say it in all kindness, because we are the best of friends personally-that it is an exceedingly bad habit he has got into of thinking that no other man ever heard of a railroad case, and that he is the encyclopaedia of railroad law. And I want to tell him that the longer he talks the more completely he dispels that impression.

I cannot agree with this proposed amendment, because I think it leaves the law still very defective. I have always taken the ground that it is an improper provision in the law which compels the farmer to keep his cattle within an enclosure if they happen to be within half a mile of the railway. I come from a section of the country that, until of recent years was comparatively a wilderness and where most of the cattle were grazed in the bush. When a farmer owns a hundred acres of land for which he paid and which happens to be unenclosed, it seems most unjust to deprive

him of the right of pasturing his cattle on that property because the railway happens to be within half a mile. When, the amendment was made to the law before, I believed it wrong, and I believe so still. Let me refer to a portion of Ontario where the land is not all agricultural land. I speak of Mani-toulin Island. Many years ago, the government of the province of Ontario sent men furnished with grass and clover seed to seed down that Island. This was done that the land might furnish grazing ground for the farmers. Perhaps eight-tenths of the land of that island can never be cultivatable. There are one or two charters in existence giving parties the right to build railways across that island. Suppose these railways are built, what are the farmers to do ? This land is not enclosed, but is rough, rocky land, good pasture because it has been seeded down, but not cultivable. Are the farmers to be deprived of the advantage of pasturing their cattle there because a railway company happens to build a railway across the island ? I say that would be unreasonable. This clause, if it is pasesd, will unduly deprive the farmers of Manitoulin of the right they now enjoy. Again, in New Ontario, where railways are being pushed for colonization purposes, you will find a thousand acres unfenced for every acre fenced. The farmers who go there as pioneers are taking in cattle in large numbers, and these cattle will be grazing in the bush year after year until the land is cleared and fenced in. Perhaps, for twenty years that will be the case. But, as soon as a railway extends into that new section, the farmers will be in danger of having their cattle impounded if they use for pasture the land they have purchased from the government and for which they have paid. Then I come to the North-west. Passing through there last fall I found that cattle in thousands and tens of thousands were being pastured upon the prairie. Every farmer who allowed his cattle to run there was violating the law. These men have taken up their homesteads, in some instances have bought their pre-emptions, but on account of this provision in the law they are not able to enjoy their property. I say the onus should be put upon the railway company and not upon the farmers. So far as this amendment changes the old law, it does not meet the requirements of the case. To that extent the law will still be defective unless It is amended so as to provide that the railway company shall fence their line, and that the farmer shall have the right to allow his cattle to run at large on the highway or on his own property, or on lands that are not tit for cultivation.
Would it be a breach of this law for a farmer in the North-west to let his cattle run on the prairies ?
It would be, if they were within half a mile of the railway.
Does the hon. gentleman know that we have a special law in the North-west Territories ?

Your herd law makes no difference, it only provides for herding cattle. But there are not perhaps ten per cent of the farmers going into that new country who have any enclosure for their cattle.
Mr. DOUGLASi The hon. gentleman does not understand the law in the North-west. That law provides that when cattle appear upon the track, either by night or by day, the railway engineers have to slow their train or blow the whistle, whether there is any person in charge of the cattle or not, and if the railway destroys the cattle it has to pay the damages.

Suppose they do both, tind cattle are killed, does the hon. member not think that the farmer who allowed his cattle to graze upon the highway within half a mile of the railroad, is violating this section ?

It must be remembered that there is no highway in the case, the farmer lias not got the highway, so the argument of the hon. member is wholly inapplicable. The farmer does not buy the highway, if he allows his cattle to stray on the highway and feed upon it, we are not doing an injury to the farmer if we ask him to keep them off half a mile from the railroad.
The hon. member says they have no highway in that country.

No, they have highways, and where there are highways this law is applicable. The hon. member referred to the Manitoulin Islands, a rocky country that cannot be fenced. He may take us all over the Dominion, but it is not possible to frame a law that will apply to every kind of country and protect the interests of the farmer. If these people cannot fence their land they are in the same position as the people in the Territories, and we cannot hope to frame a law that will be applicable to every foot of the prairie country. I see no objection to the application of the law

If the hon. gentleman is through asking a question-I think I have the floor. I want to say to the hon. member that I have conversed with many farmers in his own country, and they hold exactly the same opinion with regard to this as I do, they believe that they are unfairly ciealt with on account of this law, that they are restricted in their rights. In the province of Ontario to-day, over four-fiftlis of its area, the farmer under this law cannot. enjoy the rights to which he is fairly entitled. There is only a small portion of Ontario to-day that is old-eettled and well fenced, and wherever highways exist within

half a mile of a railway, if a farmer allows Uis cattle to be at large on that highway and they stray off, his cattle are liable to be impounded under this law.

It must be gratifying to members on both sides of the House that we have now come to a conclusion upon what is probably the most difficult point to	deal	with	in connection	with	thisBill. I appreciate the way the Minister of Railways and Canals put it when he	said	that	we need not	have	any
cleavage witli regard to party in this matter. I think we can all feel pleased that we have come to a pretty good understanding. Now the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), who initiated the agitation with regard to this matter in this House, and who has done more than any one else to keep it prominently before the public, I feel inclined to accept his suggestion, being satisfied he has given a great deal of consideration to the case, and in consequence I feel inclined to accept the amendment proposed by the bon. member for Essex .(Mr. Sutherland). I understand that substantially it embodies the idea which the member for Lincoln has been advocating during three sessions. Recognizing his leadership, and I am proud to he under his leadership in this matter, I am inclined to accept his suggestions. I acknowledge also that the Minister of Railways and Canals has bestowed a large amount of care and attention -upon this Bill, although in some cases he does not appear to have had as complete a grasp of the situation as we could wish. Although the member for Lincoln has been for three years endeavouring to remedy this evil, the member for Essex has to-night brought in an amendment which I think meets the case. It does not matter who it is that voices the principle, who it is that frames the words, so long as they secure the object we have in view. We are all in exceedingly good humour, and I have to congratulate the hon. member for Lincoln upon his complete success to-night. I feel like placing myself on record on this amendment. I think the amendment proposed by the hon. minister is amply sufficient to meet all the rights and interests of the farmers. It is carefully drawn, and I think it places a proper burden upon the railway company and gives proper relief for the farmer. It leaves the burden of proof upon the farmer that he has not been negligent in taking care of his cattle. I think that burden of proof should be on him, because the knowledge is within him alone. It was upon the same principle that we placed the burden of proof upon the railway companies Of showing that they had proper fire screens in their smokestacks and that the screens had not been punched out. We put the burden of proof upon them because the knowledge of the matter is within the railway company. There is one feature of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) which I object to, and it is the feature which puts the burden of proof upon the railway, because it would be almost impossible, in many cases, for the railroad company to become possessed of the facts. Now, it does seem to me that lion, gentlemen upon- both sides of the House, in their zeal to protect the interests of the farmers, which is most commendable, have forgotten a very important class of

people, and those are the employees of the railway companies and the travelling public. I think it Is proper legislation to put upon each party, that is the farmer and the railway company, the strongest obligation possible that they will keep their cattle and their trains from coming into contact, because, there is damage not only to the cattle of the farmer and damage not only to the rolling stock of the company, but there is danger to the lives and property of the public and servants of the railway company. Therefore, if we leave the burden upon the farmer of seeing that his cattle have not improperly strayed upon the land of the railway company, I think that is all that is required. As regards the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) surely he will not undertake to convince us that the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Essex does not meet that case entirely and completely. I was glad to see that in one sense he was ready to adopt the amendment that was proposed by the bon. member for North Essex, but it does seem to me that when he tried to propose that little amendment which would have no effect whatever, he was not acting in accordance with his professions. There is only one question that I would desire now to ask the committee to consider earnestly as I deem it to be one of the greatest importance. That is, are we acting in the interests of the farmers when we relieve them from a reasonable care, and place the burden of proving that they have not been careful upon the shoulders of parties who may not be able to prove that at all, because the knowledge will be entirely within the farmer himself? If the farmer has not been negligent it is the easiest thing in the world for him to prove it. A short time ago I brought action against a railway company for a farmer for the destruction of a herd of cattle. He had not been negligent although his cattle had escaped upon the highway, and the court so found, and he recovered damages for his cattle. So he will always recover. But when you put it the other way, you are not only putting the railway company at a disadvantage, and I do not care so much about that, but you are putting the travelling public and the employees on the railway train also at a disadvantage.

The hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) has asked again and again w-hy the words were inserted in 237 ' from straying on the railway.' He got quite excited over the propriety of my having inserted these words in this Bill. It is quite true that the words are not in the existing law, but the main proposition in the existing law is that Which requires that the animals shall be properly attended by competent persons. The fact that the words were added, that a competent person should be in charge so as to prevent the animals loitering on such highway or straying on the railway, only indicates what might happen if this competent attendance were not provided. The hon. gentleman said I put in these words because of the possibility of the animals straying on the railway owing to there being no cattle guards there. Well, there are two or three reasons why it might be well to indicate What the cattle should be prevented from doing. We know as a matter of fact that cattle-guards are not always placed on the railway. The protection of the public requires that that attendance should be there to prevent the cattle going on the railway, even if there is no cattle-guard. The interest involved is not only the interest of the farmer if his animal happens to get killed, or the interest of the railway company. The Interest of the public is in preventing the animals going on the railway so as to avoid injury to property and perhaps

loss of life. AA'e know that there are not always cattle-guards, and even if there are, we know also that these guards are not absolutely perfect in their operation, and do not provide absolute protection. In spite of the cattle-guards, animals are able to effect an entrance on the company's property, so that in any case it is well that the public should be notified that their business is to have proper attendance to look after the cattle when at the point of intersection, and that if they do not look after them, they may stray on the railway and be killed. Apart from all that, there would be no reason in asking that these words be struck out, because the section which I have moved, if carried, would fix the liability of the company, quite irrespective of whether the attendance were there or not, because that section provided that the railway company would be liable if the farmer had not been negligent. So that either with the amendment which the committee has adopted or with the amendment which I proposed before its adoption, the effect of these words or the language of this clause would not have the slightest bearing. I cannot therefore see any good reason why this amendment should be adopted. It is quite unnecessary, and I would object very strongly to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Just one point, I think, has not been touched upon in regard to the amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). I do not think the farmers themselves are anxious that their cattle should stray on the road. If they turn their cattle out improperly on the highway, and they stray on the railway and get killed, I do not think they should recover money from the railway company. But there are occasions, as everybody knows when cattle will break out of their pastures and get on to the highways, and if they do, is the farmer to have four or five men to look after them ? The farmer does not know that they are on the highway, and it would be impossible to prove that they got there through any negligence on his part. Farmers sometimes pasture their cattle a long distance from home, and the cattle, being anxious to get back home, will break through the best of fences. So that we want to provide that if they do get on the highway without the farmers' knowledge or consent, and are killed, he will have redress if there are no cattle-guards.	[DOT]

The Minister of Railways has in effect told us that these words, ' or straying upon the highway ' are harmless, that they have very little effect except for the purpose of pointing out the condition of affairs, and that, having regard to the amendment which we have just adopted, they cannot do any harm.
They would not do any harm anyway. They are only descriptive.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am of a different opinion. The section as it was before had a specific meaning, that was, that there was to be some competent person in charge of the cattle for the purpose of taking them across the railway at the point of intersection and preventing them loitering on the highway. That is the principle upon which we have worked for many years. It is the correct principle. It has nothing to do with the question of cattle-guards. AVe have defined within what limits the company shall be liable, and within what limits the proprietor shall have a right to recover; but if we leave these words in, we open the door to litigation, and the old difficulties will be repeated, it may be with this variation, that the proprietor will be more likely to win than he was in the past. AVhat this parliament should do now and for ever, if it possibly can, is to prevent this for ever-recurring litigation, and this uncertainty as to the rights of the people. If you leave these words in, the effect is this. You say to the railway company and to the public, on either hand, and although with one hand we extend protection to the farmers in the way of cattle-guards, with the other hand we bring in this clause, which means that it is not necessary for the railway company to have sufficient cattle-guards. That is in line with what the minister says. He says it may happen that the cattle-guards will not be sufficient. I say we have provided that the railway companies must have sufficient cattle-guards; that was the o'ld law and presumably the new law of to-night, and if you leave in the statute the words that are now there to prevent the cattle straying on the railway, you mean that they will stray there because there is nothing to prevent them, and you induce the railway company to set up the defence that notwithstanding the other provisions of the Act, there is no absolute liability on their part to have safe and sufficient cattle-guards at the point of intersection.

AVill the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question ? Does he not think that it is possible to imagine on behalf of the railway company such a thing as excusable negligence. This is what we have provided for on behalf of the farmer. Is it not also possible in regard to the railway company in relation to cattle-guards.
It is, but I fail to see what effect that has on my argument.

I will point out. In a case of excusable negligence where the railway company did not have proper cattle-guards, these words ' or straying on the railway,' would be not only applicable, but very necessary.

AA7hat I am endeavouring to point out is this, that if the other provision is to work out in the way I think it will, the railway company will be excused in the case where the court and jury think



they ought to be excused. What we are dealing with here is the provision that when cattle are being driven along the highway they shall be in charge of some person for the'purpose of preventing their stopping or loitering upon the railway crossings, and not for the purpose of excusing the railway companies for not having fences or cattle-guards. We will be renewing the old troubles if you enact this legislation in its present shape. I shall not urge this matter any further. I have discharged my duty and I am confident that my statements will be verified by the results. I have wai'ned the government, and I warn hon. gentlemen opposite as well. They have adopted tonight the principle which has been agitated during the last two sessions by hon. members on this side, and if it is not a case of stealing thunder from this side and merely wanting to make a show, they will have to face the music and vote for this amendment.

In reply to the hon. gentleman, let me say that I do not want to steal his thunder, but I am going to vote against this amendment. I represent a county in which there are as many highway crossings by railways as in any county in the Dominion, and probably more. It is the centre of the Grand Trunk lines at the Niagara frontier, but I have ever held that I would not support any proposition which would allow farmers to let their cattle run at large on the public highway within a half mile of the railway track. I have continually opposed that. I opposed it when the Bill of the hon. member for Lincoln was before the committee. I there gave my reasons for believing that this Bill was wrong, and the same reasons still exist. In my opinion, the proposition of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to-night was a fairer one than the motion made by the hon. member for North Essex, which the committee saw fit to adopt. So far as the present amendment is concerned, it simply suggests that three words be stricken out of this clause. This would dispense with the necessity of having cattle in charge of a competent person to prevent their straying on to the railway track. But there must be, under the section, a competent person in charge of the cattle, when they are within half a mile of the railway, and even, under the amendment of the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland), the farmer, whose cattle were not in charge of a competent person, and were destroyed at the intersection between a highway and a railway, cannot recover damage. If the cattle are in charge of a competent person, that person can without difficulty keep them off the right of way, and that is what he should do. If he does not, I do not think the farmer should get compensation. But, if cattle accidently get on the public highway and then stray on to the railway track, Mr. LENNOX.
because of insufficient cattle-guards, then the farmer should be compensated. That is the proposition I have always supported and support to-night, but I am strongly convinced that if cattle are on the highway, within half a mile of the junction of the highway with the railway, they should be iu charge of a competent individual who will prevent their straying on to the track.

The hon. gentleman seems to urge that having a competent person in charge to prevent cattle loitering upon the intersection is the same tiling as having a competent person to prevent their straying on to the railroad track. It is an entirely different matter, and that is one of the points where the difficulty comes in. One small boy may be quite sufficient to prevent a herd of cattle from stopping or loitering on the intersection of a railway with a highway, where there are proper cattle-guards, but he would be .wholly incompetent to control them where there are 110 cattle-guards.

I am sorry that I must differ from hon. gentlemen on this side. This section has been on the statutes over fifty years. Some thirty-live years ago a county judge, in the county of Brant, I think, placed a construction upon it which has not been followed by any other judge in. Ontario since. Dozens of decisions are in the books upon the meaning of this section. As to the term ' person in charge ' the courts for years have held that the person must' be one competent to take care of cattle and prevent them from loitering. Therefore putting the word < competent ' in does not add anything to the law as construed by the courts, but simply expresses in plain English what the section means. As to the other words, about straying upon the railway property, it has been distinctly held over and over again that the section would have the same result without those words. Courts have held that a cow or horse which is loitering upon a railway crossing without being in charge of some one, is illegally there ; and if it then strays upon the railway track, the owner cannot recover. Therefore, the courts have held that the meaning of the original section is precisely as if the term ' competent person ' were in it and as if these words * straying on the railway' were there also.	[DOT]

I must say, in reply to the hon. member for Hamilton, that he has misapprehended what I have been saying upon the question. 1 attach no significance to the word ' competent.' What I have endeavoured to point out is that to provide that persons must be in charge to prevent cattle from loitering upon a railway at its intersection with the highway, is an entirely different thing from providing that there 1 shall be such a force in charge as will pre-

vent them, where there Is an opening upon either side, from straying up and down the railway track. The hon. gentleman says that there are quite a number of decisions in the case of animals killed at the intersection.
No, I said that the same law applied where they strayed over the iriiiway track and were killed there.

If the hon. gentleman had waited I would have said that too. I am quite prepared to accept what the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) said with regard to the legal liability. But the reason I attach importance to these words- particularly bearing in mind the enactment we have so far adopted, and the probable result of these enactments-is that it means, if it means anything that these decisions will no longer prevail.

On section 197-fences, gates and cattle-guards.

I wish to propose an amendment which I am not sure that hon. gentlemen on the other side have seen the minister about, as I have not heard any suggestion from the minister or any body else that the amendment was necessary. I think, however, in view of the decision rendered by the Supreme Court about a year and a half ago, hon. members will consider it that some such amendment as this is needed. The case is that of James vs. Grand Trunk Railway Company, arising in the county of Wentworth, in the township of Saltfleet. I do not know whether the minister's attention has been drawn to it, but, if he does not say that it has I will go on and explain. The result of that case is to put a very queer construction upon these sections of the law, a construction which, I am sure, parliament never intended. The courts of Ontario held unanimously on one side. His Lordship Judge Street tried the case, and the court of appeal of Ontario unanimously confirmed his decision, that the fences to be built between the railway and the adjoining property are boundary fences. The present Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, then Mr. Justice Tacli-ereau, concurred in the decision of the court of appeal. He said he could not see but that the reasons given by the court of appeal of Ontario were unassailable. But the other four judges of the Supreme Court thought differently, and put a very narrow construction upon the law, a construction not intended by parliament, I feel sure. Now the words of this section are the words of the old law

The report of Judge Street is to be found in Ontario reports, volume 31, and that judgment was confirmed by the court of appeal in which Chief Justice Armour, justices Osier and Lister wrote judgments, and Justice Moss, the present chief justice agreeing but not writing any language of his own. The case that arose is this : What might have been used as a cattle-pass if so arranged, but was a water-course which was dry in summer, ran under the railway track. The railway company, instead of fencing across that and continuing their line fence between the ad-

In the ease which the Supreme Court adjudicated upon and which the hon. gentleman has mentioned, the cattle strayed through and under one of the company's culverts and got around upon their right of way and on the track because there was no fence placed along the railway at that place. They left this open space in their fences through which the cattle strayed upon the property of other people and ultimately got upon the company's lands. Now it would be thought that under the law as it stands to-day the railway company were bound to fence along their line so that cattle could not get upon their track; that is the spirit and intention of the Act. This decision we have to accept as good law, but we have made ample provision in the present Bill for all that. The law now makes the company liable for all cattle lost that were straying from the adjoining land, whether they have got a fence ten feet high or not. Whether the fence is on the division line or not, the company has got to pay for cattle which get upon its right of way from adjoining lands. The reason of that is because we wanted to remove the possibility of any of these questions arising which have prevented owners of cattle from getting damages from the company because their cattle had strayed off on to other lands and from those other lands had got upon the railway. I say the company is bound to pay for cattle killed^or Injured upon the railway, where they have strayed off on adjoining lands.

speechtext: Where is the declaration that applies to adjoining owners ?
The law provides that the fences must be suitable and sufficient to keep the cattle.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The law provided that when this decision of the Supreme Court was given, but it is the kind of fences that was involved and where they should be, and the Supreme Court has decided that these fences need not be sufficient to keep the cattle from getting under the track but only sufficient to keep them from getting over it. Now, the declaration that they must have these fences was the same before the Supreme Court gave that decision.
They never provided that in the previous law.

speechtext:
The previous section had exactly the same words; of course there were other words in the section that are not applicable to this point. Section 194, the old statute, says :
Fences shall be erected and maintained on each side of the railway through each township, of the height and strength of an ordinary division fence.
The court said that these words ' fences ' of the height of an ordinary division fence ' with proper gates and fastenings, were not sufficient. Now the words * fences on each side of the railway,' were the words when the Supreme Court gave that decision, and the court has held that fences on each side of the railway do not protect the farmer from his animals getting under the track but only upon the surface.
In this amended Bill there are entirely different words used which would seem to exactly meet the point that has been decided.
What section of the Bill 1
Subsection 2 of section 197 says that the fences are to be suitable and sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway.

These words were in the old law.
Fences shall be erected and maintained on each sfde of the railway, through such township, of the height and strength of an ordinary division fence, with openings or gates or bars or sliding or hurdle gates of sufficient width for the purposes thereof, with proper fastenings at farm crossings of the railway, and also cattle-guards at all highway crossings suitable and sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway.
The provision was virtually the same as we have It in the Bill :
Fences, of a minimum height of four feet six Inches, on each side of the railway, and swing, or sliding gates, therein, of the said minimum height, with proper fastenings, at farm crossings.
1 Mr. RUSSELL. I was looking at the old Act and I find that the language is hot the same as it is in the Bill which is. before the committee. If it had been, it
seems to me that would have been a surprising decision for the Supreme Court to give. The Supreme Court and the court of appeal both agree that the fences were to be sufficient to prevent the animals from getting on the railway track, but what the Supreme Court said was that they need not be sufficient to keep them off the other railway property.
I do not wonder at the hon. gentleman being very much surprised at the judgment given.
