What reason would there be in saying that providing the railway has sufficient fences to keep cattle getting on the railway they must in addition to that have fences to prevent cattle from getting under the railway ?
: Mr. LANCASTER. I will tell the hon. gentleman what happened in the James case and it will happen in other cases unless the railway company makes provision against it. Mr. James owned land at one side of the railway and another man owned land on the other side of the railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That does not make any difference.
: Mr. LANCASTER. It does make a difference to the man who loses his animals. The hon. minister does not care about that, but I do. Mr. James thought that the company were bound to fence against him. They did not fence the culvert. Water ran through in the spring, but in the summer it was

dry. The railway company chose to stop fencing when they got to the culvert and ran the fence in at half right angles to the culvert. The result was that Hr. James' animals got upon a neighbour's property, the neighbour did not keep the gate shut and they got upon the highway and got into trouble.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When all the facts and circumstances are looked at there must have been some question about their straying on the property of the railway company and there must have been some question of contributory negligence on the part of the owner. When the law says that a railway company must fence so as to prevent cattle from getting upon the railway, if they do fence sufficiently and the cattle are prevented no damage can occur. If they do not do that and the cattle are killed upon the railway they are liable. Somebody has to take the responsibility of deciding whether the hon. gentleman is right or whether I am right. The hon. gentleman has stated his position and there is no occasion for him to repeat it over and over again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is if the hon. minister does not understand me.

If the hon. minister will look at Mr. Justice Sedgewick's decision he will see that the hon. member for Lincoln is quite wrong. Mr. Justice Sedge-wick in his decision said:
The horses in question were admitted to be at large upon the highwaj within half a mile of its intersection with the line of railway. They were in charge of no one so as to prevent their loitering or stopping on the highway at the point of intersection. It was at that point they were killed and the owner has not therefore any right of action by reason of such killing.

I think both hon. gentlemen are right. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) says quite correctly that the animals had escaped under the railway to a neighbour's farm, thence to the highway and thence upon the railway; so that, both provisions of the law came in. I would like to suggest to my hon. friend from Lincoln to consider what would be the effect upon a large number of farmers if the railway were fenced in the way he proposes. The hon. gentleman must know that there are many farmers who have the privilege of allowing their cattle to pass under the small culverts and bridges from one side of the railway to the other. This is of very great value indeed and if you compel the railway company to fence out all these places the balance of convenience would be vastly against a large number of farmers.
How could a horse or a cow be billed if the railway erected proper fences to prevent cattle from getting upon their right of way ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If you compel the railway company to fence its gullies and valleys the farmer who has a valuable privilege in allowing his cattle to pass through will be deprived of that. There are a great many streams that the railway will have to fence and it is almost impossible to do that.

Of course, as the hon. minister says, this is a matter for which he has taken responsibility and having directed his attention to it I will be satisfied to leave it at that. The point, I understand that is involved in the case that is referred to or that arises under this subsection is as to what the meaning of the words contained in this subsection is :
Such fences and gates shall be suitable and sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway.
I do not pretend to be familiar with the case that has been cited, although I knew that it had been decided. A somewhat startling decision was given by the Supreme Court reversing the decision of the court of appeal. It is provided definitely enough that they must have sufficient fences to prevent cattle getting on the railway, and the only possible way in which the Supreme Court could come to a conclusion, that this is not a complete provision for a continuous fence along each side of the railway property, is that it speaks of the railway as distinct from the railway property. I happen to have been told the opinion of some of the judges of the Court of Appeal on that Supreme Court judgment, and that is the only way, as I understand it that, they can account for it. By the use of the word ' railway ' as distinguished from the words ' railway property ' it may be that the railway company was not under the old Act compelled to make a continuous fence from one end of their property to the other. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) always presents his views in a very moderate and well-considered way and there is no doubt much as to what he says in reference to the inconvenience that might in some instances arise. One case which I have in mind is this :	I have a property
on one side of the railway which is rented to a farmer and a Mr. Cook has a property on the other side. There is a large bridge with stone abutments and a stream of considerable size. The railway company does not continue their fence across this stream and the result is that the cattle of one farmer cross the stream and get on the farm of the other and there is constant difficulty between them. One of these farmers has been driving the cattle that improperly came upon his land on to the highway, and if the cattle wandered a quarter of a mile further and got on to the level crossing and are killed, the railway company woufd not be liable although the original cause of the cattle being on the highway was that they did not carry a continuous fence along their

property. Cases of this kind must necessarily arise and it would be well to have this matter dealt with.
I could not do what the hon. gentleman suggests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will not press it upon the minister unduly. I have no doubt that the minister has taken great care in the consideration of this matter, but I would submit to him that provision should be made for the case in the nature I have indicated. If the wording of the new Act is the same as the old, the judgment of the Supreme Court will continue to prevail until there is an appeal to the Privy Council; which might reverse it. An hon. gentleman on the other side (Mr. Russell) for whose opinion I have the very greatest respect says that the wording in this section is different from the wording of the old. I will not take time in arguing the point, but I may say, that while the grouping of thf clauses is different, I do not see any difference in the wording.

I happen to be interested in a property on which there are 350 yards of a viaduct and it is a very valuable privilege to have free access under this viaduct by reason of the fact that the railway has no fence on either side of this land.
1	know of half a dozen other instances where the same privilege now exists. The people own the property on both sides of the bed of the river and they go freely under the viaduct whereas if fences were there it would be a great inconvenience to them.

I would take the liberty of moving some slight amendments. I move to insert after the word ' cattle-guards ' in the fifth clause, the words ' approved of by the board,' and to strike out of subsection
2	the words * and cattle-guards.' My reason for asking for that is this, that as the section is now framed we are asking an impossibility of the company. It is perfectly proper to ask them to have a fence sufficient to keep the cattle off the road; but it has been demonstrated by a commission during the past year, what we all knew before, that it is impossible to get a cattle-guard which will keep the cattle off the road. Therefore I submit that it is unfair to put that section in, and I would ask the minister to accept this amendment. It seems to me that it is fair and reasonable.
The difficulty is that you have defined in another section what a fence is to be.

I propose to amend the clauses so as to say that the cattle-guards shall be approved by the board, and the fences and gates shall be sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from gettiug on the railway.

In view of the amendment which we have passed already, I do
not think it is necessary to amend this section in the way proposed.

I think the hon. gentleman has doubtless judged that the disposition of the committee is rather unfriendly to his motion.
Amendment of Mr. Wade negatived, and amendment of the Minister of Railways agreed to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I propose to strike out some words in the third division of section 197 with reference to gates. On still further consideration, I think it would be better to leave it to the commission to judge whether hinges or sliding gates are the proper kind of gates, and if they find that they are not, they have the power under the Bill to condemn them and to specify what other gates shall be used. I propose that the clause shall read :
Swing gates and such fences of the minimum height aforesaid, with proper fastenings, at farm crossings, provided that sliding or hurdle gates already constructed may he maintained but shall not hereafter be renewed If so ordered by the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the minister make it read, ' unless ordered by the board,' so that the farmers will not have to come to Ottawa to get the permission of the board ?

I think it is better as it is. It will let the existing conditions continue, unless the board orders otherwise. I have correspondence upon the subject from people who are decidedly opposed to doing away with the hurdle gates, and who say that they are very useful.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That would require immediate action, if you had hurdle gates In order to continue them. If the merits are against their continued use, the board will determine not to allow them.
Mr. BARKER, What the hon. gentleman-would like is to put it upon the railway companies to obtain the permission and not upon the farmers to object. If a company wanted permission to renew the gates, they would have to apply to the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is the difference between the two propositions. I must confess to a decided preference for my method. These gates have been used for years and we are hearing now, for the first time of any complaint. Is it desirable that we should proceed upon the assumption that the objections are well taken ? I do not think they are, and we ought to allow the condition of

things to continue until the board has satisfied itself that it ought not to continue.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 198,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I move that the following be substituted for this section :
Whenever a railway passes through any locality in which the lands on either side are not improved by settlers and inclosed, the company shall not be required to erect and maintain such fences, gates and cattle-guards unless the board otherwise orders or directs.
That was the law before.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: By what section was it the law before ? The law was that where a township was opened up and set apart for settlement, the railways were bound to fence. According to this section, if you happen to strike a couple of vacant lots on either side of the railway, the company will not be bound to fence unless the board directs it.
How would it do to say ' district ' instead of ' locality,' and say ' on both sides.'

The principle is this, and it is the law everywhere else if not in Ontario. If an owner of land has cleared his ground, he would naturally put up his fences and the company would have to fence in front and on their right of way. I cannot see any advantage in requiring a fence to be erected on the other side of the track, if there is no settlement and nothing but an unoccupied wilderness.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The cattle will be pasturing on both sides although the people are living only on one side.

It is not a question of wilderness, but of a vacant lot on each side of the railway. In such a case the railway company shall not be bound to fence unless ordered by the board. Take this case. There is a property of say 200 acres, which has not been cleared or improved. It belongs to some one who does not reside in the neighbourhood. There is running across the further end of that lot a - public highway. On that public highway the cattle are allowed to run and they cannot approach within half a mile of the railway. They stray into that vacant property from the highway thence get on to the track and are killed, and the owner has no redress. This is another way of minimizing the benefits we are getting for the farmers through the fight we are putting up in their behalf. It is a most unfair proposal.

You might go to Ontario, even the old settled parts, and you would find large sections of swamp lands where some of the lots are unoccupied. A farmer Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
could not allow his cattle out to graze on the highway or this unsettled land without the danger of having his cattle killed, and under this clause he would have no redress. In the newer settlements, every farmer turns his cattle out into the bush and they run at large, in any direction. If the company is not compelled to fence its property, they will be sure to get on to the track, and if injured, the owner has no recourse. This will be a great injustice to the farmer who is the pioneer of the country.

I do not think that the case is serious at all. In sections of the country such as are described here, there are no fences, and you never hear of cattle being killed. They are not so apt to stray on to the railway tracks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can tell the hon. minister that if he will allow forty-eight hours delay, I will get twenty-five or thirty cases from the county I represent where animals have been killed on the track under just such circumstances as would make it impossible, if this amendment passed for the owners to get a dollar. For instance, go into the township of Proton, in the countv of Grey or Amaranth or Melancthon, where the large swamps are, though it is an old settled country. The same danger would exist there in many places.

There is not a township in the province of Ontario in which cases could not be found of this kind. I think that we should not, without good and sufficient cause, depart from the old form of the statute. The law was sufficiently favourable to the railway companies and afforded no more than enough protection to the people. There is no good reason advanced for the proposed change. I venture to say that the people, not only in Ontario, but of the whole Dominion, will be surprised when they learn to-morrow morning that such a proposition was made. If the hon. minister will allow this to stand for forty-eight hours, we can have petitions here from every part of Ontario against anv such legislation.
Amendment (Hon. Mr. Blair) agreed to. Yeas, 22 ; nays, 10.

This Bill has been amended so many times-and I suppose it was necessary-that it is almost impossible to keep track of it. I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any provision in it for the better protection of level crossings in towns, cities and villages.
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by ' better protection.' Complete and ample protection is provided for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Is any change to be made in the existing law to give -better protection at railway crossings.
The MINISTER OB' RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I think perhaps it might be said to be improved somewhat in that regard.
Perhaps the hon. minister would tell us in what respect it is improved ?

We have given the board full power to require anything and everything that they may deem necessary for the protection of these crossings. We have not confined them or limited them in any way. It would be impossible, I think, to employ language which would give ampler control than is given the board under the Bill. It is possible that the Railway Committee of the Privy Council may have been a little derelict in its duty, so far as the exercise of its power in this respect was concerned. It may have been that their opportunities of going about the country and seeing how the different localities were protected were not sufficient. That might be a reason why they would not be as likely to give this protection in as full and ample a measure as the proposed commission would be likely to do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would ask the minister to consider this clause :
Every company shall provide and maintain at all level crossings within cities, towns and villages whether incorporated or otherwise, such gates, electric bells or subways as may be sufficient for the protection of persons using the streets or highways.
Let me give the hon. minister an example of the need that exists for better protection than is now afforded. The Grand Trunk Company has expended a large sum on their main line between Toronto and Hamilton, and now that company, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who also use the line, are running very fast trains between Hamilton and Toronto. At the different railway crossings in my own county and others between Hamilton and Toronto the danger is considerably increased. In the villages along the lake shore, like Port Credit, customers coming have to cross the railway. I understand that in this present Bill, the hon. minister has provided that a railway company shall have the right to run trains through a town not merely at six miles an hour, as under! the present law but at ten miles an hour. Yet he has made no provision for further protection for passers-by at the railway crossings.
That protection is to he provided by the board, and the board has been empowered to do the very things the hon. gentleman lias mentioned in liis amendment. AVe cannot do more than that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We could put it in the Bill and make it law, instead of leaving it to the board.

It would not be made any more law than we have already made it. The hon. gentleman wants to put in the Bill a provision that a railway company shall be compelled to provide suitable and sufficient-or words equivalent to that-protection by means of gates, watchmen, or some other method. But that is the law now. Somebody must determine when it is necessary that there shall be more protection and what form that protection is to take. If you re-enact it a dozen times, you give it no more power. I can assure the hon. gentleman his amendment is not necessai'y. At the same time I recognize the necessity that ample power should be conferred upon the board in these matters. But we have already provided for that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. minister answer this one question ? Under the Bill as it is before the House now, is it provided that the crossings- shall be better protected than under the old Railway Act ? I cannot understand it if it is so.
Under the enactment of this Bill, they may be better protected.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It depends entirely upon the good will of the board.
The MINISTER OB" RAILWAYS AND CANALS. You could not gain anything by simply passing a section providing that street crossings on the level shall he better protected than they are now. On the other hand, you cannot make the clause more definite or complete than that which has been passed by the committee. There are differences in the requirements of different localities and in the protection needed. . Some need less, and some need more.
I would suggest that he insert the words ' or watchman.'
I am opposed to this amendment, not because it is not necessary, but because the provisions are already covered by existing enactments.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Tbe minister means that because the board has power to order these things they are all there ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is not the same thing as to the proposed amendment. The amendment makes these provisions obligatory. In the one case this parliament is delegating to the board power to do what they may think fit; in the other case we are laying down a rule to guide the board.
Amendment negatived.

The subject of these side ladders has been much considered by me. I had the benefit of hearing people representing the railways and some representing the operatives, and I felt much embarrassed in trying to come to a conclusion as to whether the disadvantages or the advantages of the side ladders preponderated. The more I heard on the question the more I felt that this parliament was not capable of determining a question of that kind, but that the board, which is to be charged with these duties could much better be trusted to settle this question. Now, we have under our general railway law given full power to the board, which Is authorized to see that all proper appliances are provided for the safety of the employees; they must see that the trains are safely equipped, and that the appliances are altered from time to time when in their judgment they may deem it necessary. When we here require that a particular sort of appliance should be adopted we are making it imperative upon the companies that they should continue to adopt these appliances and a continual change in the railway law of this parliament will be required In order that the improvements should be in general use. That is not a desirable state of things. I think the object would be much better served by leaving this contentious question to be determined by the board, which could take the best means of ascertaining what are the real facts of the matter. Therefore, I would urge the hon. gentleman not to press the motion he has mentioned here, because I think it is one we would not be justified in adopting.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If the hon. minister will say that the law should not be as the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram)

has stated, that these ladders should not be on the ears, I would agree that we should not put this amendment in, but X cannot agree with bis reason that we should refrain from adopting such a provision because we might have to repeal this provision if some better contrivance were found in future. It would not be any more trouble to do so than to pass some of the private Bills that go through this House pretty hurriedly sometimes and some of which involve in some ways much larger questions than this.

I have heard both sides, and I have not been able to make up my mind one way or the other. I was far from concluding that it would be a safe thing to do because, we know where engines are shunting trains in the yards and where the cars are approaching one another, taking all the precautions1 that you can, persons who are hanging on the side of the car, perhaps on a dark night, might be struck and if they are struck they would likely be fatally struck under such circumstances. There are various reasons that could be urged against it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All of which do not amount to anything.
After listening to the discussion as closely as I could, I was unable to reach a satisfactory conclusion in my own mind. Therefore, I could not recommend the committee to adopt the amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the 200 and odd members of this House could come to a conclusion upon this question with the information that the hon. minister has in his possession. I think we are delegating a great deal too much to this board. I think we will require 300 men and not three to carry out all that we are delegating to the board. It was never contemplated in the beginning that we were going to delegate everything to this board.
I do not think this parliament is well equipped to determine such a question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There may be somethings, of course, such as the question of preventing discrimination in rates, that we want the board to deal with, but questions in regard to mechanical appliances should not be referred to the board. If the board is to be bothered with matters of that kind and is expected to give attention to them in the same way that another commission would I do not think it will have much time to deal with some of the important questions referred to it. If the hon. minister proposed to refer this question to two or three men to report to this House I could see some sense in a reference of that kind for the purpose of gathering the facts. It
was even suggested seriously by an hon. gentleman on the opposite side that we should leave it to the commission to say what shall be a suitable and sufficient cattle-guard. If this board is not able to do its work well it will be our fault because we have imposed so many duties upon it. If we do agree that these ladders should be put upon the cars it would be well to say so in the Bill as proposed by the hon. member for East Elgin.

It seems to me that the parties above all others who will either be benefited or injured by this appliance are the train men, and if they desire it they should have it because they are the people who are running the danger all the time. They are the parties who would be injured in the event of the appliance being an improper one, but practical experience convinces them that it would be a benefit to them.
They do not agree.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The very fact that the number of resolutions mentioned by the hon. member for East Elgin has been passed is pretty conclusive evidence that the great bulk of the employees of the companies do agree as to the advisability of adopting that appliance and I think we ought to accept that as sufficient. It is not something that is very expensive to the companies, and therefore it could not be objectionable upon that ground.

the railway employees residing in their particular constituencies are very strong upon this line of legislation. The hon. minister speaks of referring this question to the board. If the hon. gentleman will look at section 211 he will see that he has specifically defined matters of equipment that must be provided. What greater injustice would it be to specify this particular class of equipment in the same way as the others are specified ? If the request of the employees, who are certainly the ones interested as it is a matter of life and death to them, is granted, it will impose, it is true, some expense upon the railway companies. These side ladders are for trains not for yards, and when the gentlemen in the committee mentioned about the difficulty of getting up on the side ladders they did not know what they were talking about. They professed to be railway officials but they had prejudiced minds. The yardmen are very little on top of the cars in the yards, but every one knows that the trainmen of this country have risk enough to undergo without imposing risks on them that can be avoided. I have simply done my duty in carrying out the request of the gentleman from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) and backing, it up with my personal opinion on this legis-' lation. Having done that the responsibility must rest with the minister and the government for refusing these men the legislation that they have passed some sixty resolutions in favour of.

I agree with what the hon. gentleman from Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has said. I happen to represent a large railway centre and the men asked that a Bill of this kind should be passed, and some years ago I took up the question. We were told then that it should be delayed until we saw the result of the experiment in the United States, but we are no further ahead to-day than we were seven or eight years ago. In the United States they gave the railway companies a certain number of years to provide safety equipment and the brakemen in the United States are in consequence in a better position than they are in Canada.
It is useless to leave this to a board to haggle over; the only proper thing to do . is to put it in a law in the statute-book. The Brotherhood of Trainmen have passed resolutions all through the Dominion in favour of this, and it is time we should pay some heed to the request of men who risk ' their lives in the operations of railways in i this country.	i
opinion from the employees opposed to this Bill, and I may say that expressions of opinion coming from companies professing to give the opinion of the employees on a measure of this kind, should always be taken with a great deal of caution. On this particular section there had been an attempt made to have the employees give expressions of opinion against this Bill, and out of 211 men, 210 were in favour of it, and one did not care, because, as he said, it did not affect him. It is my experience that the men are unanimously in favour of this Bill. My opinion is that included among safety appliances there should be a full length rail on the top edge of box cars. This rail would give a chance to the man grasping at something, should he fall, and in the matter of life and death like this, we should give the railway employee every possible chance. As a matter of fact, wherever expense is to be incurred, the railway companies are very apt not to carry out the suggestions of the men. I do not think the railway companies would have any cause of complaint if we ordered this, and I do not think that the expense would amount to much. Neither do I think that . the opposition of the railway companies ought to be given too much weight in a matter of this kind, and 1 trust that the Minister of Railways will see his way to introduce this provision for the safety of the men.

This matter was fully threshed out, and statements were made pro and con, and I do not hesitate to say that there was by no means any satisfactory evidence that this appliance had been determined upon as suitable or as in the interests of the employees of the railway. The Master Car Builders' Association represents the interests of all who are running trains, and this association have enforced the use throughout the United States of almost every safety appliance that was necessary in the interests of. the employees. They are regarded as an association of such authority, that the law of most of the states of the union declares that what they endorse as a proper appliance must be used upon the cars. They have not approved of this side ladder.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That was in the evidence, but I would like to see the proof of that statement. In the interchange of foreign cars the side ladders are used.

There is no room for doubt as to the position of the railway employees on this question. For the last two years this matter has been before the trainmen, and I have never heard any objection on the part of the employees to this Bill. I was recently on one of the sections of a large company in the east, where an attempt had been made to get an expression of Mr. INGRAM.

In the interchange of American cars there are some with side ladders and some without, and the Master Car Builders' Association have not required the side ladder. It has been left an open question, and that shows that the association has not been able to conclude that it was a device which would add additional safety to the men.

The fact that the cars that are coming into this country and the cars that are in this country are not uniform in this respect is an important consideration to be taken into account in the passage of such a law as this. We ought not to require that these ladders should be placed on our cars when innumerable cars are coming from the United States in the course of traffic which have not these ladders upon them. If they all had the ladders, I presume that the danger would be minimized. But as there are probably as many ears without ladders as with them, if we required all cars to have them on, we would have to exclude the cars from the United States, or we would subject the employees to still greater dangers. It is a question which we ought to be very cautious about legislating upon. It is all very well to say that some association has called upon us to do it; but these local associations do not exhaust the subject, and do not always come to right conclusions. If this device was all that is claimed for it by my hon. friend opposite, the Master Car Builders' Association would have adopted it in the United States. I do not think we need discuss the matter further. The hon. gentleman has stated his case and I have replied, and I think we might now pass the clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This may not be a very important question to the hon. gentleman, but it is a serious question to the railway employees of this country. It is a matter of life and death to them; and when the hon. gentleman undertakes to reflect upon the intelligence of the trainmen of this country and tells them that they do not know what they want, I think he is going entirely too far.
What does the hon. gentleman mean ? I did not say that they did not know what they were talking about, and I would thank the hon. gentleman not to put words in my mouth which I did not use.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am simply drawing an inference from what the hon. gentleman said.
You have no right to draw that inference.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When a question comes up in this House involving the rights of the workingmen of this country and is treated in a sneering manner by some hon. gentlemen opposite, I want to say that these men have as much right to be treated with consideration in this parliament as any other men.
I have as much consideration for the rights and interests of the workingmen as the hon. gentleman has.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then the hon. gentleman should not try to prevent me putting their case before this House. Who are the master car builders ? They are mechanics who have worked in the workshops of this country. Many of them never mounted a car in their life. The trainmen who are mounting the cars night and day, in fair weather and bad weather, who take their lives in their hands, are to be told that they do not know how to mount these cars, but that they must mount them in the most dangerous way, forsooth, because the master car builders do not favour these side ladders. I know from personal experience the inconvenience that these men have to suffer. I have thousands of times mounted the railway cars of this country, and I am not ashamed of it. While doing that I associated with just as intelligent men as those I have associated with in this House-men who are as capable of understanding their requirements as hon. gentlemen in this House are capable of understanding theirs. There are college-bred men occupying positions on trains in this country, men who are as capable to be representatives in this House as hon. gentlemen who are here. And are these men to be told that they do not know what they want, that they are entirely mistaken, and that the Master Car Builders' Association know better what they require than they do themselves ? I tell you it is a matter of life and death to these men. It may be of more interest to the hon. gentleman to have the railway companies pay larger dividends instead of supplying the things that are necessary to protect the lives and limbs of their employees. I have read all this evidence given by certain railway -officials, and I say that the statements made there are not justified by the facts. I challenge the hon. minister to appoint a special committee and have the railway .employees come here, and see whether these statements are true or false. It is all very well for the large corporations to oppose side ladders because they have adopted end ladders. All I have to say is that if the employees do not know better than the companies what they require, then God help the employees. I have nothing to say against the railway companies, because it is as much in their interest to protect their employees, and not have loss of life and limb from time to time. Hon. gentlemen will find, if they look at the statistics, that railway employees have suffered accidents either by falling off cars or by coupling cars. I do feel indignant when I am told that I have stated my case once or twice, and that ought to be sufficient. When the general election comes round and that is the time these men look for redress, they will inquire from their representative whether he is Grit or Tory, if he has supported this legislation, and they will tell him that they look upon it as an important piece of legislation and such as

justify them in only voting for candidates who will support the legislation they require.

We are dealing with a Bill governing railway matters. We have introduced clauses to protect shareholders, bondholders, farmers and passengers. The proposal is now made, at the request of the railway men, that certain clauses ought to be put in the Bill for the protection of the men who operate these railways, and we are told that we are wasting time in considering their rights. X protest against that and appeal to the hen. Minister of Labour whether it is not his duty to see that the men who work upon these trains are protected. They have asked year after year parliament to intervene. I introduced legislation in this respect years ago, but on one argument or another it was always side-tracked, and no progress made. Every time I brought It up, some insufficient reason has been given why adequate protection should not be afforded the men who operated the roads. I appeal to the hon. minister, if he is not in a position to give an answer now, to take time to consider this question, which involves the lives and safety of those men. Similar protection is given in other countries. In England the main feature of railway legislation is to secure the safety of the lives of the public and the men who operate the train, and the result is that there are fewer railway accidents in England than in any other country. This is largely due to the fact that parliament has made such provision as will not only protect the lives of the passengers but of the men who operate the trains.

I have no reason to continue the discussion any later and we might as well stop at this stage. It is very evident that I cannot get the Bill finally disposed of tonight, and I therefore move that the committee report progress and ask leave to sit again.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When will the Bill be taken up again ?

It will be the first order at our next sitting.
Progress reported.
The MINISTER OP FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What will be the business for to-morrow ?
This Railway Bill and one or two Bills on the Order Paper that may be dealt with, and if we reach Supply we will take up the estimates of the Department of the Interior.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 1.40 a.m. Thursday.
Thursday, July 9, 1903.
